title: I. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner well known in our district in his day, and still remembered here because of his gloomy and violent death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I'll describe in its proper place. For now I'll only say that this “landowner”—as we used to call him, though he barely spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange sort, yet one you run into fairly often: abject and vicious, and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless men who are perfectly capable of managing their worldly affairs, and, it seemed, of nothing else. Fyodor Pavlovitch, for instance, started out with next to nothing; his estate was tiny; he ran around dining at other men's tables, sponging off them like a hanger-on, and yet by the time he died it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in cash. And all the while he remained one of the most senseless, fantastical men in the whole district. I repeat, it wasn't stupidity—most of these fantastical men are shrewd and intelligent enough—it was simply senselessness, a peculiar, homegrown kind of it.

He was married twice, and had three sons: the eldest, Dmitri, by his first wife, and two more, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, came from a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, also landowners in our district—the Miüsovs. How it happened that an heiress, and a beauty besides, one of those vigorous, intelligent girls so common in this generation but sometimes found in the last one too, could have married such a worthless, puny weakling as we all called him, I won't try to explain. I once knew a young lady of that last “romantic” generation who, after years of a mysterious passion for a man she could easily have married at any moment, invented insurmountable obstacles to their union and ended by throwing herself, on a stormy night, into a rather deep, fast river from a high bank—almost a cliff—and perished there, purely to satisfy her own whim, to be like Shakespeare's Ophelia. In fact, if that cliff, her favorite chosen spot, had been less picturesque—if there had been an ordinary flat bank there instead—the suicide probably would never have happened. That's a fact, and there have surely been more than a few similar cases in the last two or three generations. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov's action was, no doubt, likewise an echo of other people's ideas, brought on by the irritation of having no mental freedom of her own. She wanted, perhaps, to show her independence as a woman, to rise above class distinctions and her family's tyranny. And a pliable imagination convinced her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, despite his parasitic standing, was one of the bold, ironic spirits of that progressive age—when in fact he was nothing but an ill-natured buffoon. What gave the marriage its spice was that it was preceded by an elopement, and this captivated Adelaïda Ivanovna's imagination completely. Fyodor Pavlovitch's position at the time made him especially eager for any such venture, since he was desperate to make a career for himself one way or another. Attaching himself to a good family and getting a dowry was an alluring prospect. As for mutual love, there was apparently none of it, not on the bride's side and not on his, despite Adelaïda Ivanovna's beauty. This was, perhaps, a unique case in the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch, a man of an always lustful temperament, ready to chase after any skirt at the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the one woman who made no particular appeal to his senses.

Immediately after the elopement Adelaïda Ivanovna realized in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. The marriage showed its true colors with extraordinary speed. Although her family accepted the affair fairly quickly and settled her dowry on the runaway bride, husband and wife began leading a thoroughly disorderly life, and there were endless scenes between them. It was said that the young wife showed far more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch, who, as we now know, got hold of all her money—up to twenty-five thousand roubles—the moment she received it, so that sum was lost to her forever. The little village and the rather fine town house that made up the rest of her dowry he did his utmost, for a long time, to transfer into his own name by means of some deed of conveyance. He probably would have succeeded, simply from her moral exhaustion and her desire to be rid of him, and from the contempt and disgust his persistent, shameless pestering aroused in her. But luckily Adelaïda Ivanovna's family stepped in and blocked his greed. It's known for a fact that there were frequent fights between husband and wife, but rumor had it that Fyodor Pavlovitch did not beat his wife, but was beaten by her, since she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. In the end she left the house and ran off from Fyodor Pavlovitch with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a three-year-old, in her husband's hands. Fyodor Pavlovitch promptly installed a regular harem in the house and gave himself over to drunken orgies. In the intervals he would drive all over the province, weeping to everyone about Adelaïda Ivanovna having left him, going into details too shameful for a husband to mention about his own married life. What seemed to please him most, flattering his vanity, was playing the ridiculous role of the wronged husband and parading his sorrows with embellishments.

“Anyone would think you'd gotten a promotion, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you seem so pleased despite your grief,” mockers said to him. Many even added that he was glad of a new comic role in which to play the buffoon, and that it was precisely to make it funnier that he pretended not to notice his ridiculous position. But who knows—it may just have been simplicity. At last he managed to track down his runaway wife. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had gone with her divinity student and had thrown herself into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once began bustling about, making preparations to go to Petersburg—for what purpose he couldn't have said himself. He probably would have actually gone; but having decided to go, he felt entitled at once to fortify himself for the trip with another bout of reckless drinking. And it was just then that his wife's family received news of her death in Petersburg. She had died suddenly, in a garret—of typhus, according to one story, or, as another version had it, of starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife's death, and the story goes that he ran out into the street and began shouting for joy, raising his hands to heaven: “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace,” though others say he wept without restraint, like a small child, so much so that people felt sorry for him despite the revulsion he inspired. It's entirely possible both versions were true—that he rejoiced at his release and at the same time wept for the woman who had released him. As a rule, people, even wicked ones, are far more naive and simple-hearted than we assume. And so are we ourselves, for that matter.

title: II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: You can easily imagine what kind of father a man like that would make, and how he'd raise his children. His conduct as a father was exactly what you'd expect. He completely abandoned the child from his marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna—not out of malice, and not because of some grudge over the marriage, but simply because he forgot about him. While he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints, and turning his house into a den of debauchery, a loyal family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya under his wing. If he hadn't looked after him, there would have been no one even to change the baby's shirt.

It happened, too, that the child's relatives on his mother's side forgot about him at first as well. His grandfather was no longer living, his grandmother—Mitya's grandmother—had moved to Moscow and was seriously ill, and his aunts were all married, so Mitya spent almost a whole year in old Grigory's care, living with him in the servants' cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (and he couldn't have been entirely unaware of his existence), he would only have sent him back to the cottage, since the child would just have been in the way of his debaucheries. But a cousin of Mitya's mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, happened to return from Paris around then. He would go on to live abroad for many years afterward, but at the time he was quite a young man, notable among the Miüsovs for his enlightened views and European polish, a man who had lived in the capitals and abroad. By the end of his life he had become a Liberal of the type common in the forties and fifties. Over the course of his career he'd come into contact with many of the most progressive men of his time, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally, and in his later years loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he himself had very nearly taken part in the fighting on the barricades. This was one of the most cherished memories of his youth. He had an independent fortune of about a thousand serfs, to use the old reckoning. His splendid estate lay on the outskirts of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery, with which Pyotr Alexandrovitch, almost as soon as he came into the property, began an endless lawsuit—over fishing rights on the river, or timber rights in the forest, I don't know exactly which. He considered it his duty as a citizen and a man of culture to launch an attack on the “clericals.” Hearing all about Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom he of course remembered and had once been interested in, and learning that Mitya existed, he stepped in—despite all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He made the man's acquaintance for the first time, and told him directly that he wished to take charge of the child's education. He liked to tell, long afterward, as a telling detail, how when he first brought up Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch looked at him for a while as though he didn't understand which child was being discussed, and even seemed surprised to learn he had a little son living in the house. The story may have been exaggerated, but it must have been something close to the truth.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was fond, all his life, of playacting, of suddenly taking on some unexpected role, sometimes for no reason at all, even to his own direct disadvantage—as, for instance, in this very case. This habit, though, is characteristic of a good many people, including some quite clever ones, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the matter through energetically, and was appointed, together with Fyodor Pavlovitch, joint guardian of the child, who had a small property—a house and some land—left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin's care, but since the cousin had no family of his own, and, having secured the income from his estate, was in a hurry to get back to Paris, he left the boy in the charge of one of his own cousins, a lady living in Moscow. As it turned out, once he'd settled permanently in Paris, he too forgot about the child, especially once the February Revolution broke out and made such an impression on him that he remembered it for the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed into the care of one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time after that. I won't go into it further now, since I'll have much more to say later about Fyodor Pavlovitch's firstborn, and for now I must confine myself to the most essential facts about him, without which I couldn't begin my story.

In the first place, this Mitya, or rather Dmitri Fyodorovitch, was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch's three sons who grew up believing he had property of his own, and that he'd be independent once he came of age. He spent an irregular boyhood and youth. He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium; he got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was busted down to the ranks, earned his rank back, lived wildly, and spent a good deal of money. He received no income at all from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then ran up debts. He saw and met his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the first time upon coming of age, when he visited our neighborhood specifically to settle accounts with him over the property. He doesn't seem to have liked his father. He didn't stay with him long, and hurried to get away, having only managed to obtain a sum of money and an agreement for future payments from the estate—the revenue and value of which he was unable, notably, to get any accounting of from his father on this occasion. Fyodor Pavlovitch noted for the first time then (this too is worth noting) that Mitya had a vague and inflated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was quite pleased about this, since it suited his own designs perfectly. He gathered only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, violent-tempered, impatient, and dissipated, and that if he could just get hold of ready cash he'd be satisfied—for a short while, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began exploiting this, sending him small doles and installments from time to time. In the end, four years later, when Mitya, out of patience, came a second time to our little town to settle things once and for all with his father, it turned out, to his astonishment, that he had nothing left—that it was hard even to get an accounting—that he had already received the full value of his property in sums of money from Fyodor Pavlovitch, and might even be in debt to him, that by various agreements he'd entered into of his own free will at various earlier dates, he had no right to expect anything more, and so on and so forth. The young man was overwhelmed, suspected fraud and cheating, and was nearly beside himself. And indeed, this circumstance led to the catastrophe that forms the subject of my first introductory story—or rather, its outward side. But before I get to that story, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch's other two sons, and where they came from.

title: III. The Second Marriage And The Second Family
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Very shortly after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married a second time. This second marriage lasted eight years. He took this second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, also a very young girl, from another province, where he'd gone on some small piece of business together with a Jewish associate. Though Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, he never once neglected investing his capital, and he managed his business affairs very successfully—though not, admittedly, very scrupulously. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon, and was left an orphan from childhood, without relatives. She grew up in the household of a general's widow, a wealthy old lady of good standing who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I don't know the details, but I've heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a noose she'd hung from a nail in the attic—so unbearable were her sufferings from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who wasn't at heart bad-natured but had become an insufferable tyrant out of sheer idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch proposed to her; inquiries were made about him, and he was turned down. But again, as with his first marriage, he suggested an elopement to the orphan girl. There's very little doubt she'd never have married him at all if she'd known a bit more about him in time. But she lived in another province, and besides, what could a sixteen-year-old girl know, except that she'd be better off at the bottom of the river than staying with her benefactress? So the poor child traded a benefactress for a benefactor. This time Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't get a penny, since the general's widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he hadn't been counting on a dowry; what drew him was the girl's remarkable beauty, above all her innocent look, which had a particular appeal for a depraved libertine who up to then had admired only the coarser kinds of feminine beauty.

“Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor,” he used to say afterward, with his revolting snigger. In a man so depraved this might, of course, mean nothing more than a sensual attraction. Since he'd gotten no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her “off the noose,” he didn't stand on ceremony with her. Making her feel that she'd “wronged” him, he took advantage of her extraordinary meekness and submissiveness to trample on the most basic decencies of marriage. He gathered loose women into his house and carried on drunken orgies right in front of his wife. To show what things had come to, I might mention that Grigory—the gloomy, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna—took the side of his new one. He championed her cause, cursing out Fyodor Pavlovitch in a manner hardly fitting for a servant, and on one occasion broke up the revels and drove all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end, this unhappy young woman, terrorized since childhood, fell into the kind of nervous illness most often found in peasant women said to be “possessed by devils.” At times, after terrible fits of hysterics, she even lost her mind. And yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey—the eldest in the first year of the marriage, the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year, and, strange as it seems, I know that he remembered his mother his whole life—like a dream, of course. When she died, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as had happened to their elder brother, Mitya. They were completely forgotten and abandoned by their father. They too were looked after by Grigory, and lived in his cottage, where they were found by the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother. She was still alive, and hadn't, in all those eight years, forgotten the insult done to her. The whole time she had kept herself exactly informed of Sofya's way of life, and hearing of her illness and her hideous surroundings, she declared aloud two or three times to her servants:
“It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna's death, the general's widow suddenly turned up in our town and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. She spent only half an hour in town, but she got a great deal done. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom she hadn't seen in those eight years, came in to meet her drunk. The story goes that, the moment she saw him, without a word of explanation, she gave him two good, resounding slaps across the face, seized him by a tuft of hair, and shook him up and down three times. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. Seeing at a glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, she promptly boxed Grigory's ears too, and, announcing that she would take both children away with her, wrapped them just as they were in a blanket, put them in her carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory took the blow like a devoted servant, without a word, and when he escorted the old lady to her carriage he gave her a low bow and solemnly declared that “God would repay her for the orphans.” “You're a blockhead all the same,” the old lady shouted back at him as she drove away.

Thinking it over, Fyodor Pavlovitch decided this was all for the best, and didn't refuse the general's widow his formal consent to whatever she proposed regarding his children's education. As for the slaps she'd given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

It happened that the old lady died soon after this, but she left the boys a thousand roubles each in her will, “for their education, and to be spent on them exclusively, on condition that it be so allotted as to last until they turn twenty-one, since it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people see fit to throw their money away, let them.” I haven't read the will myself, but I've heard it was worded oddly in places, very whimsically. The main heir, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the provincial Marshal of Nobility, turned out, however, to be an honest man. Writing to Fyodor Pavlovitch, and seeing at once that nothing could be extracted from him for his children's education (though the man never directly refused, but simply stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even at times gushingly sentimental about it), Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the orphans. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long while as one of his own family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. To Yefim Petrovitch—a man of a generosity and humanity rarely met with—the young men owed more for their upbringing and education than to anyone else. He kept the two thousand roubles left to them by the general's widow intact, so that by the time they came of age their shares had doubled through accumulated interest. He educated both of them at his own expense, and certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I won't give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth here, but will mention only a few of the most important events. Of the elder, Ivan, I'll only say that he grew into a somewhat morose, withdrawn boy, though far from timid. By the age of ten he'd already realized that they were living not in their own home but on other people's charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful even to speak of. This boy began very early—almost in infancy, they say—to show a brilliant and unusual gift for learning. I don't know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch's household when he was barely thirteen, entering a Moscow gymnasium and boarding with an experienced, well-known teacher, an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch's. Ivan used to claim afterward that all this was due to Yefim Petrovitch's “zeal for good works,” who was taken with the idea that the boy's genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor that teacher was still alive. Since Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady's legacy, which had by then grown from one thousand to two, it was held up by the usual bureaucratic delays inevitable in Russia, and the young man found himself in serious straits during his first two years at the university, forced to support himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he made no attempt to contact his father—whether out of pride, or contempt for him, or simply his cool common sense telling him he'd get no real help from such a father. Whatever the case, the young man didn't despair in the slightest, and managed to find work, at first giving lessons at sixpence a time, then getting paragraphs about street incidents placed in the newspapers under the byline “Eye-Witness.” These pieces, it was said, were so lively and sharp that they were soon in demand. This alone showed the young man's practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, luckless students of both sexes who hang about newspaper and magazine offices, unable to come up with anything better than endless pleading for copying work or French translations. Once he'd gotten in with the editors, Ivan Fyodorovitch kept up the connection, and in his final years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialist subjects, so that he became known in literary circles. But it was only in his last year that he suddenly succeeded in catching the attention of a much wider circle of readers, so that a great many people noticed and remembered his name. It was a rather curious episode. Just as he'd left the university and was preparing to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, Ivan Fyodorovitch published, in one of the leading journals, a strange article that attracted general notice—on a subject he might have been assumed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. The article dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the position of the ecclesiastical courts. After running through several existing opinions on the subject, he went on to set out his own view. What was most striking about the article was its tone, and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him unquestioningly for one of their own. And yet not only the secularists but even the atheists joined in applauding him. In the end some shrewd observers concluded that the article was nothing but an impudent, satirical piece of burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article found its way into our famous local monastery, where the monks, being especially interested in the question of ecclesiastical courts, were left thoroughly baffled by it. Learning the author's name, they took an interest in the fact that he was a native of the town, and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And it was just then that the author himself turned up among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come to us I remember asking myself at the time, with a certain unease. This fateful visit, which would set off so many consequences, I never fully explained to myself. It seemed odd, on the face of it, that a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so cautious, would suddenly turn up at such an infamous household, at the home of a father who had ignored him his whole life, barely knew him, never gave him a thought, and would never under any circumstances have given him money—though he was always afraid his sons Ivan and Alexey would come asking him for some. And here was the young man staying in the house of such a father, having lived with him for two months already, on the best of terms. This last fact was a particular source of wonder to many others besides me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, whom we've already mentioned, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, happened to be in the district again, visiting his estate. He'd come from Paris, which was his permanent home. I remember he was more surprised than anyone when he made the young man's acquaintance—Ivan interested him enormously, and Miüsov sometimes argued with him and, not without a pang, compared himself against him in terms of learning.

“He's proud,” he used to say, “he'll never be short of money; he's got enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Anyone can see he hasn't come for the money, since his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink or dissipation, and yet his father can't do without him. The two of them get along so well!”

That was the truth: the young man clearly had influence over his father, who genuinely seemed to be behaving more decently, and even at times seemed ready to obey his son—though often extremely, even spitefully, contrary.

It was only later that we learned Ivan had come partly at the request, and in the interests, of his elder brother Dmitri, whom he was seeing for the first time on this very visit, though he'd been in correspondence with him before leaving Moscow about an important matter that concerned Dmitri more than himself. What that matter was, the reader will learn fully in due course. Yet even once I knew of this particular circumstance, I still found Ivan Fyodorovitch an enigmatic figure, and thought his visit rather mysterious.

I might add that Ivan appeared, at the time, in the role of mediator between his father and his elder brother Dmitri, who was in open conflict with his father and even planning to bring a lawsuit against him.

The family, I repeat, was now gathered together for the first time, and some of its members were meeting one another for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us for a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It's of this brother, Alexey, that I find it hardest to speak in this introduction. And yet I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one odd fact—that I have to introduce my hero to the reader wearing the cassock of a novice. Yes, he'd spent the last year in our monastery, and seemed prepared to be cloistered there for the rest of his life.

title: IV. The Third Son, Alyosha
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: He was only twenty; his brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, while their elder brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First, I should explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic, and, in my opinion at least, wasn't even a mystic. I might as well give my full opinion right from the start. He was simply an early lover of humanity, and the reason he took up monastic life was simply that, at the time, it struck him as the ideal escape for a soul struggling out of the darkness of worldly wickedness into the light of love. And the reason this life struck him that way was that he found in it, as he thought, an extraordinary being: our celebrated elder, Zossima, to whom he attached himself with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. But I don't dispute that he was very strange even then, and had been from the cradle. I've already mentioned, by the way, that though he lost his mother in his fourth year, he remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses—“as though she stood alive before me.” Such memories can persist, as everyone knows, from an even earlier age, from as young as two, but they scarcely stand out across a whole lifetime like isolated points of light in the darkness, like a corner torn out of some vast picture that has otherwise faded and vanished, save for that one fragment. That's how it was with him. He remembered one still summer evening: an open window, the slanting rays of the setting sun—that he recalled most vividly of all—in a corner of the room the holy icon, a lamp burning before it, and, kneeling before the icon, his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying out and moaning, snatching him up in both arms and squeezing him so tightly it hurt, praying for him to the Mother of God, holding him out with both arms toward the icon as if to place him under the Mother's protection… and then suddenly a nurse rushing in and snatching him away from her in fright. That was the picture. And Alyosha remembered his mother's face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied, but beautiful, as he remembered it. But he rarely cared to speak of this memory to anyone. As a child and a young man he wasn't at all expansive, and talked very little, but not out of shyness or sullen unsociability—quite the opposite—it came from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, entirely personal and unconcerned with other people, but so important to him that he seemed, in a sense, to forget about them because of it. But he was fond of people; he seemed, his whole life, to place implicit trust in them, and yet no one ever took him for a simpleton or a naive fool. There was something about him that made you feel at once—and it stayed true all his life afterward—that he had no wish to judge others, that he would never take it upon himself to criticize or condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the slightest condemnation, though often grieving bitterly over it, and this was so pronounced that no one could ever shock or unsettle him, even in his earliest youth. Arriving at twenty in his father's house—a veritable sink of filthy debauchery—he, chaste and pure as he was, simply withdrew in silence when the sight became unbearable, but without a trace of contempt or condemnation. His father, who had once been in a dependent position himself and was thus touchy and quick to take offense, met him at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn't say much,” he used to remark, “and thinks all the more.” But soon—within a fortnight, in fact—he took to hugging and kissing him constantly, with drunken tears and maudlin sentimentality, and yet he plainly felt a real, deep affection for him, of a kind he'd never before been capable of feeling for anyone.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and it had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, so that they came to regard him quite as their own child. Yet he'd entered the house at such a tender age that he couldn't possibly have acted out of calculation or cunning in winning their affection. So the gift of making himself loved, directly and unconsciously, was simply built into him, into his very nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed at first glance to be exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes mock, even dislike. He was dreamy, for instance, and rather solitary. From his earliest childhood he loved to creep off into a corner with a book, and yet he was a general favorite the whole time he was at school. He was rarely playful or lighthearted, but anyone could see at a glance that this wasn't sullenness. On the contrary, he was bright and good-natured. He never tried to show off in front of the other boys. Perhaps because of this he was never afraid of anyone, and yet the boys understood right away that he wasn't proud of his own fearlessness, that he seemed unaware he was bold and brave at all. He never held a grudge over an insult. It might happen that an hour after being wronged he'd speak to the one who'd wronged him, or answer some question of his, with as trusting and open an expression as if nothing had passed between them. And it wasn't that he seemed to have forgotten the slight, or deliberately forgiven it—he simply didn't regard it as a slight at all, and this utterly won the boys over. He had one trait that made every one of his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to tease him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. This trait was a wild, almost fanatical modesty and chastity. He couldn't bear to hear certain words, certain conversations about women. There are “certain” words and conversations that, unfortunately, can never quite be stamped out in schools. Boys pure in mind and heart, practically children still, love to talk among themselves, even out loud, about things, pictures, images that even soldiers would sometimes hesitate to mention. More than that, a good deal that soldiers know nothing of is entirely familiar to quite young children of our educated, upper classes. There's no real moral depravity in it, no genuine corrupt cynicism at its core, but there's the appearance of it, and it's often treated among them as something refined, daring, subtle—worth imitating. Seeing that Alyosha Karamazov stuck his fingers in his ears whenever they started on “that,” they'd sometimes crowd round him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears, while he struggled, slid to the floor, tried to hide, without ever uttering a word of abuse, enduring the insult in silence. But eventually they left him alone, and stopped taunting him as a “regular girl”—in fact they came to regard it, with something like pity, as a weakness in him. He was always among the top students in his class, but never first.

By the time Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha had two more years to finish at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow went almost immediately after his death on a long trip to Italy with her whole household—which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha went to live in the home of two distant relatives of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies he'd never even met before. On what terms he lived with them, he didn't know himself. It was very characteristic of him, in fact, that he never worried about at whose expense he was living. In this he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who'd struggled through poverty during his first two years at university, supporting himself by his own efforts, and who'd been bitterly aware since childhood that he was living off his benefactor's charity. But this odd trait in Alyosha's character shouldn't, I think, be judged too harshly, because the moment you got to know him even slightly, you'd have seen that Alyosha was one of those youths—almost of the religious-enthusiast type—who, if they suddenly came into a large fortune, wouldn't hesitate to give it all away at the first asking, whether for good works or to some clever con artist. In general he seemed hardly to know the value of money—not literally, of course. When given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it, so that it vanished in a moment, or else he'd hold onto it for weeks on end, not knowing what to do with it.
In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very touchy on the subject of money and bourgeois respectability, delivered the following judgment after getting to know Alyosha:

“Here, perhaps, is the one man in the world you could leave alone without a penny in the middle of an unfamiliar city of a million people, and he wouldn't come to any harm—he wouldn't die of cold or hunger, because someone would feed and shelter him at once; and if they didn't, he'd find shelter for himself, and it wouldn't cost him any effort or any humiliation. And sheltering him would be no burden to anyone—quite the opposite, it would probably be seen as a pleasure.”

He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium. A year before the end of the course, he suddenly announced to the ladies that he was going to see his father about a plan that had occurred to him. They were sorry, and reluctant to let him go. The trip wasn't an expensive one, and the ladies wouldn't let him pawn his watch, a parting gift from his benefactor's family. They provided him generously with money, and even outfitted him with new clothes and linen. But he returned half the money they gave him, saying he intended to travel third class. On arriving in town he gave no answer to his father's first question about why he'd come before finishing his studies, and seemed, so people said, unusually thoughtful. It soon became clear he was looking for his mother's grave. He more or less admitted, at the time, that this was the sole reason for his visit. But that can hardly have been the whole of it. It's more likely that he himself didn't understand, and couldn't explain, what had suddenly stirred in his soul and drawn him irresistibly onto a new, unknown, but inevitable path. Fyodor Pavlovitch couldn't show him where his second wife was buried, since he'd never once visited her grave after throwing earth onto her coffin, and over the years had entirely forgotten where she lay.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, incidentally, hadn't been living in our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife's death he'd gone off to the south of Russia and eventually turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. He made the acquaintance, at first, in his own words, “of a bunch of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and ended up being received by “Jews high and low alike.” It's a fair guess that this is the period when he developed his particular knack for making and hoarding money. He finally returned to our town only three years before Alyosha's arrival. His old acquaintances found him looking terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man yet. He carried himself not exactly with more dignity, but with more brazenness. The former buffoon now showed an insolent tendency to make buffoons out of other people. His depravity with women hadn't simply stayed the same—it had grown even more repulsive. In short order he opened a large number of new taverns across the district. It was clear he had something like a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many people in town and the surrounding district were soon in his debt, and had, of course, put up good security. Lately, too, he'd grown somehow bloated, and seemed more erratic, more uneven, had sunk into a kind of incoherence, would start one thing and carry on with another, as though he were letting himself go entirely. He was drunk more and more often. And if it hadn't been for that same servant, Grigory—who by now had aged a good deal himself, and sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor—Fyodor Pavlovitch might have gotten into serious trouble. Alyosha's arrival seemed to affect even his moral side, as though something long dead in this prematurely old man's soul had stirred back to life.

“Do you know,” he'd often say, looking at Alyosha, “that you're like her, ‘the crazy woman'”—that's what he used to call his dead wife, Alyosha's mother. It was Grigory who pointed the “crazy woman's” grave out to Alyosha. He took him to our town cemetery and showed him, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone—cheap but decently kept—with the name and age of the deceased and the date of her death inscribed on it, and below, a four-line verse of the kind commonly used on old-fashioned middle-class graves. To Alyosha's astonishment, this tombstone turned out to be Grigory's own doing. He'd put it up on the poor “crazy woman's” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch—whom he'd pestered about the grave repeatedly—had gone off to Odessa, abandoning the grave along with all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother's grave. He only listened to Grigory's detailed, solemn account of putting up the stone; he stood there with his head bowed and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he visited the cemetery again. But this small episode wasn't without its effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a rather original effect at that. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for the soul of his wife—not the second one, Alyosha's mother, the “crazy woman,” but the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, who used to beat him. That same evening he got drunk and cursed out the monks to Alyosha. He himself was far from religious; he'd probably never once put a penny candle in front of a saint's icon. Sudden bursts of feeling and sudden thoughts are common enough in men of that sort.

I've already mentioned that he looked bloated. His face at this time bore unmistakable marks of the life he'd led. Besides the long, fleshy pouches under his small, always insolent, suspicious, ironic eyes, besides the mass of fine wrinkles in his small fat face, his Adam's apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, giving him a peculiarly repulsive, sensual look; add to that a long, greedy mouth with full lips, between which you could glimpse little stumps of blackened, decayed teeth. He drooled every time he started talking. He liked, in fact, to make fun of his own face, though I believe he was perfectly satisfied with it. He was especially fond of pointing to his nose, which wasn't very large but was quite delicate and conspicuously hooked. “A proper Roman nose,” he used to say, “with my goiter I've got quite the look of an ancient Roman patrician from the age of decline.” He seemed proud of it.

Not long after visiting his mother's grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were prepared to take him in as a novice. He explained that this was his firm wish, and that he was formally asking his father's consent. The old man already knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“That's the most honest monk among them, no question,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, seeming scarcely surprised by his request. “Hm!… So that's where you want to go, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he broke into his slow, half-drunken grin, not without a certain slyness and tipsy cunning in it. “Hm!… I had a feeling you'd end up something like this. Would you believe it? You were making straight for it. Well, no matter, you've got your two thousand roubles. That's a dowry for you. And I'll never desert you, my angel. I'll pay whatever's needed for you there, if they ask for it. But if they don't ask, why should we bother them, eh? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. Hm!… Do you know that near one monastery there's a place, outside the town, where every baby in the place knows there's nothing living there but the 'monks' wives,' as they call them. Thirty women, I believe. I've been there myself. You know, it's interesting in its own way, of course, as a novelty. The worst of it is, it's terribly Russian. No French women there. Of course they could get some easily enough, they've got plenty of money. If word gets to them, they'll come running. Well, there's nothing of that sort here, no 'monks' wives,' and two hundred monks. They're honest men. They keep the fasts, I'll grant them that… Hm… So you want to be a monk? And you know, I'm sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I've really grown fond of you? Well, it's a good opportunity, though. You'll pray for us sinners; we've sinned plenty here. I've always wondered who'd pray for me, whether there's anyone in the world to do it. My dear boy, I'm awfully stupid about that. You wouldn't believe how stupid. You see, however dim-witted I am about it, I keep thinking—I keep thinking, from time to time, of course, not all the while. It's impossible, I think, for the devils to forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. And then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? Made of what? Iron hooks? Do they have some kind of foundry down there? The monks in the monastery probably believe there's a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I'm ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. It's more refined that way, more enlightened—more Lutheran, so to speak. And really, what does it matter whether it has a ceiling or not? But you know, there's a damnable question tangled up in it. If there's no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, the whole thing falls apart—which is unlikely too, since then there'd be no one to drag me down to hell, and if they don't drag me down, where's the justice in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, purpose-built for me alone, because if you only knew, Alyosha, what a scoundrel I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” said Alyosha, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That's how a Frenchman once described hell: '_J'ai vu l'ombre d'un cocher qui avec l'ombre d'une brosse frottait l'ombre d'une carrosse._' How do you know there are no hooks, my darling boy? Once you've lived with the monks you'll sing a different tune. But go and find out the truth of it there, and then come and tell me. It's easier, anyway, going into the next world if you know what's waiting for you there. Besides, it'll suit you better with the monks than here with me, with a drunken old man and young harlots—though you're like an angel, nothing touches you. And I dare say nothing will touch you there either. That's why I'm letting you go—because I'm hoping for that. You've got all your wits about you. You'll burn, and you'll burn out; you'll be healed, and come back again. And I'll be waiting for you. I feel that you're the only creature in the world who hasn't condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can't help feeling it.”
And he even started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked, and he was sentimental.

title: V. Elders
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, rapturous, poorly developed creature—a pale, consumptive dreamer. On the contrary, Alyosha at this time was a well-built, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, radiant with health. He was very handsome too, graceful, of moderate height, with dark brown hair, a regular, rather long oval face, and wide-set dark gray eyes that shone; he was very thoughtful, and yet, it seemed, very serene. I'll be told, perhaps, that red cheeks aren't incompatible with fanaticism and mysticism, but I'd say Alyosha was more of a realist than almost anyone. Oh, no doubt, in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles are never a stumbling block for the realist. It isn't miracles that predispose realists toward belief. A true realist, if he's an unbeliever, will always find the strength and the wherewithal to disbelieve in the miraculous, and if confronted with a miracle as an irrefutable fact, he'd sooner disbelieve his own senses than admit it. And even if he does admit it, he admits it as a fact of nature previously unrecognized by him. In the realist, faith doesn't spring from the miracle—the miracle springs from faith. Once the realist believes, then his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous as well. The Apostle Thomas said he wouldn't believe until he saw, but once he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not; he believed solely because he wanted to believe, and quite possibly he fully believed in the depths of his heart even as he said, “I will not believe until I see.”

I'll be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was slow-witted, undeveloped, hadn't finished his studies, and so on. That he didn't finish his studies is true, but to call him stupid or dull would be a real injustice. I'll simply repeat what I've said above. He took up this path only because, at the time, it alone caught his imagination and presented itself to him as the ideal escape for his soul from darkness into light. Add to this that he was, to some degree, a young man of our own most recent era—that is, honest by nature, craving the truth, searching for it, believing in it, wanting to serve it at once with the whole strength of his soul, seeking immediate action, and ready to sacrifice everything, even his own life, for it. Though these young men, unfortunately, fail to understand that sacrificing one's life is, in many cases, the easiest sacrifice of all, and that to give up, say, five or six years of their seething youth to hard, tedious study—if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they've set as their goal—such a sacrifice is entirely beyond the strength of many of them. Alyosha's path ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift accomplishment. As soon as he thought seriously about it, he became convinced of the existence of God and of immortality, and at once he said to himself instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I'll accept no half measures.” In just the same way, if he'd decided that God and immortality didn't exist, he'd have become an atheist and a socialist on the spot. For socialism isn't merely a question of labor—it's, above all, the question of atheism, the question of the particular shape atheism has taken in our own day, the question of the Tower of Babel built without God, not to reach heaven from earth but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

Alyosha said to himself: “I can't give two roubles instead of 'all,' and only go to mass instead of 'following Him.'” Perhaps his childhood memories brought back our monastery, where his mother might have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy icon to which his poor “crazy” mother had lifted him up still worked on his imagination. Brooding over such things, he may have come to us hoping to find out whether he could sacrifice everything here, or only “two roubles,” and it was in the monastery that he met this elder. I need to digress here to explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, and I'm sorry to say I don't feel very qualified to do so. I'll try, all the same, to give a rough sketch of it in a few words. Authorities on the subject claim that the institution of “elders” is fairly recent, no more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East—especially at Sinai and Athos—it's existed for over a thousand years. It's said to have existed in ancient Russia too, but through the calamities that befell the country—the Tartars, civil war, the break in relations with the East after Constantinople fell—the institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great “ascetics,” as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his followers. But to this day it survives in only a handful of monasteries, and has at times been treated almost as an unwelcome innovation in Russia. It flourished especially at the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our own monastery, I can't say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was nearly dying of weakness and disease, and there was no one to take his place. This was an important question for our monastery, since it hadn't up to then been distinguished by anything in particular: it had no relics of saints, no wonder-working icons, no glorious traditions, no historic exploits to its name. Its fame across all of Russia had come through its elders, whom pilgrims flocked for thousands of miles to see and hear.

What, then, was such an elder? An elder was someone who took your soul, your will, into his own soul and his own will. When you chose an elder, you renounced your own will and handed it over to him in complete submission, complete self-abnegation. This novitiate, this harsh school of self-denial, was taken on voluntarily, in the hope of self-conquest, of self-mastery, so that after a lifetime of obedience one might attain perfect freedom—that is, freedom from the self—and escape the fate of those who go through their whole lives without ever finding their true selves within themselves. This institution of elders wasn't founded on theory, but grew out of a thousand years of practice in the East. The obligations owed to an elder aren't the same as the ordinary “obedience” that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. This obligation involves confession to the elder by everyone who has submitted to him, and an unbreakable bond between him and them.

There's a story told, for instance, of the early days of Christianity: one such novice, having failed to carry out some command his elder had laid on him, left his monastery in Syria and went off to Egypt. There, after great feats of asceticism, he was found worthy at last to be tortured and put to death for the faith. When the Church, regarding him as a saint, came to bury him, suddenly, at the deacon's exhortation of “Depart, all ye unbaptized,” the coffin holding the martyr's body left its place and was cast out of the church—and this happened three times. Only at last did they learn that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and abandoned his elder, and so could not be forgiven, in spite of his great deeds, without the elder's absolution. Only after that could the burial take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here's a more recent instance.

A monk was suddenly ordered by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place, a haven of refuge, and to go first to Jerusalem to pay homage to the Holy Places, and then north to Siberia: “There is the place for thee, and not here.” The monk, overwhelmed with grief, went to the Œcumenical Patriarch in Constantinople and begged to be released from his vow of obedience. But the Patriarch answered that not only was he himself unable to release him, but there wasn't, and couldn't be, any power on earth that could release him, except the elder who had laid that duty on him in the first place. In this way, elders are endowed, in certain cases, with unlimited and inexplicable authority. That's why, in many of our monasteries, the institution was at first resisted, almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile, the elders quickly came to be held in the highest regard among ordinary people. Crowds of the uneducated poor, as well as men of distinction, flocked, for instance, to the elders of our monastery, to confess their doubts, their sins, their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and guidance. Seeing this, opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being carelessly and frivolously cheapened, though the constant opening of the heart to the elder, by monk or layman alike, had nothing whatever of the character of the sacrament about it. In the end, however, the institution of elders held on and is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It's true, perhaps, that this instrument—tested over a thousand years for the moral regeneration of a man, carrying him from slavery into freedom and toward moral perfection—can be a double-edged weapon, and may lead some not toward humility and complete self-mastery, but toward the most Satanic pride—that is, toward bondage rather than freedom.

The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners, had served in the army in his early youth, and served as an officer in the Caucasus. He must have impressed Alyosha with some particular quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the elder's cell, and the elder, who was very fond of him, let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no formal obligation, and could go wherever he pleased, and be away for whole days at a time. Though he wore the monastic habit, he did so voluntarily, simply so as not to stand apart from the others. No doubt he liked doing it. Possibly his young imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that so many people had, over the years, come to confess their sins to Father Zossima, and to beg him for words of advice and healing, that he'd developed an almost uncanny intuition, and could tell, from an unfamiliar face alone, what a newcomer wanted and what was weighing on his conscience. He sometimes astonished, even frightened, his visitors by knowing their secrets before they'd said a word.

Alyosha noticed that many—almost all—went in to the elder the first time with apprehension and unease, but came out with bright, happy faces. Alyosha was particularly struck by the fact that Father Zossima wasn't at all severe. On the contrary, he was almost always cheerful. The monks used to say he was drawn more strongly to those who were more sinful, and that the greater the sinner, the more he loved him. There were, no doubt, some among the monks, right up to the end of his life, who hated and envied him, but they were few, and they kept silent, though among them were men of considerable standing in the monastery—one, for instance, among the older monks, noted for his strict fasting and his vows of silence. But the majority stood with Father Zossima, and a great many of them loved him with all their hearts, warmly and sincerely. Some were almost fanatically devoted to him, and would say, though not quite aloud, that he was a saint—no question about it—and, seeing that his end was drawing near, they looked forward to miracles and great glory for the monastery in the near future, once his relics were there. Alyosha had unquestioning faith in the elder's miraculous power, just as he had unquestioning faith in the story of the coffin that flew out of the church. He watched many people come with sick children or relatives, begging the elder to lay hands on them and pray over them, and return shortly after—some the very next day—falling in tears at the elder's feet, thanking him for healing their sick.

Whether they'd really been healed, or had simply improved in the natural course of their illness, was a question that didn't exist for Alyosha, since he fully believed in his teacher's spiritual power, and rejoiced in his fame, in his glory, as though it were his own triumph. His heart pounded, and he practically glowed all over, when the elder came out to the gates of the hermitage into the crowd of waiting pilgrims—humble folk who'd flocked from every corner of Russia to see the elder and get his blessing. They fell down before him, wept, kissed his feet, kissed the ground he stood on, and wailed, while the women held up their children to him and brought him the sick, the “possessed by devils.” The elder spoke to them, read a short prayer over them, blessed them, and sent them on their way. Lately he'd grown so weak, from repeated bouts of illness, that he sometimes couldn't even leave his cell, and pilgrims would wait several days for him to come out. Alyosha didn't wonder why they loved him so, why they fell down before him and wept for the sheer emotion of seeing his face. He understood perfectly well that, for the humble soul of the Russian peasant, worn out by grief and toil, and even more by the endless injustice and endless sin—his own and the world's—it was the greatest need and comfort of all to find someone, something, holy, to fall down before and worship.

“Among us there's sin, injustice, temptation—but still, somewhere on earth there's someone holy and exalted. He has the truth; he knows the truth; so it isn't dead here on earth; so one day it will come to us too, and rule the whole earth, as promised.”

Alyosha knew this was exactly how the people felt—even reasoned. He understood it, but that the elder Zossima really was this saint, this custodian of God's truth—of that he had no more doubt than the weeping peasant women and the sick mothers holding out their children to the elder. His conviction that after his death the elder would bring extraordinary glory to the monastery was, if anything, stronger in Alyosha than in anyone else there, and lately a kind of deep inner flame of rapture had been burning ever more fiercely in his heart. He wasn't in the least troubled that this elder stood before him as a solitary example.

“No matter. He is holy. He carries in his heart the secret of renewal for everyone—that power which will, at last, establish truth on the earth, and then all men will be holy and love one another, and there'll be no more rich or poor, no exalted and no humbled, but all will be as children of God, and the true Kingdom of Christ will come.” That was the dream living in Alyosha's heart.

The arrival of his two brothers, whom he hadn't known before, seemed to make a deep impression on Alyosha. He made friends more quickly with his half-brother Dmitri (even though he arrived later) than with his own full brother Ivan. He was intensely interested in his brother Ivan, but even after Ivan had been in town two months, though they met fairly often, they still weren't close. Alyosha was naturally quiet, and seemed to be waiting for something, embarrassed about something, while his brother Ivan—though Alyosha noticed early on that Ivan looked at him for a long time, curiously—seemed soon to have stopped thinking about him at all. Alyosha noticed it with a certain awkwardness. At first he put his brother's indifference down to the gap in their ages and education. But he also wondered whether Ivan's lack of curiosity and warmth might stem from some other cause entirely unknown to him. He kept imagining that Ivan was absorbed in something—something inward, something important—that he was striving toward some goal, perhaps a very hard one to reach, and that this was why he had no thought to spare for him. Alyosha wondered, too, whether the learned atheist might not feel some contempt for him—a foolish novice. He knew for certain his brother was an atheist. He couldn't take offense at this possible contempt, and yet, with an uneasy embarrassment he couldn't quite explain to himself, he waited for his brother to draw closer to him. Dmitri always spoke of Ivan with the deepest respect, and with a peculiar earnestness. From him, Alyosha learned all the details of the important business that had lately created such a close, remarkable bond between the two elder brothers. Dmitri's enthusiastic remarks about Ivan struck Alyosha all the more since Dmitri was, next to Ivan, almost uneducated, and the two brothers were such a study in contrasts of personality and character that it would be hard to find two men more unlike each other.

It was around this time that the meeting—or rather, the gathering—of this discordant family's members took place in the cell of the elder who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The pretext for this gathering was a false one. It was at this time that the discord between Dmitri and his father had reached its sharpest point, and their relations had grown unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to suggest, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima's cell, and that, without appealing directly for his intervention, they might more decently come to some understanding under the elder's conciliating influence. Dmitri, who had never seen the elder, naturally assumed his father was trying to intimidate him, but, secretly blaming himself for his outbursts of temper toward his father on several recent occasions, he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he wasn't, like Ivan, staying with his father, but living separately at the other end of town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at the time, seized eagerly on the idea. A Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, he may have been driven by boredom, or by the hope of some frivolous diversion. He was suddenly struck with the desire to see the monastery and the holy man for himself. Since his lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, he used it as a pretext to see the Superior, hoping to settle it amicably. A visitor coming with such laudable intentions might be received with more attention and consideration than one who came out of mere curiosity. Influence was brought to bear from within the monastery on the elder, who had lately hardly left his cell at all, and had been forced by illness to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was fixed.
“Who made me a judge over them?” was all he said, smiling, to Alyosha.

Alyosha was greatly troubled when he heard about the planned visit. Of that whole quarrelsome, wrangling group, Dmitri was the only one who might take the interview seriously. All the others would come from frivolous motives, ones that might well insult the elder. Alyosha was well aware of that. Ivan and Miüsov would come out of curiosity, perhaps of the crudest kind, while his father might well be planning some piece of buffoonery. Though he said nothing, Alyosha understood his father through and through. The boy, I repeat, was far from as simple as everyone took him for. He awaited the day with a heavy heart. No doubt he kept turning over in his mind how the family discord might be brought to an end. But his chief worry concerned the elder. He trembled for him, for his reputation, and dreaded any affront to him—especially the refined, courteous irony of Miüsov, and the supercilious half-remarks of the highly educated Ivan. He even thought of warning the elder, telling him something about them beforehand, but on second thought said nothing. He only sent word the day before, through a friend, to his brother Dmitri, that he loved him and expected him to keep his promise. Dmitri was puzzled, since he couldn't remember having made any such promise, but he wrote back that he'd do his utmost not to let himself be provoked “by vileness,” though, even though he deeply respected the elder and his brother Ivan, he was convinced the meeting was either a trap set for him or an unworthy farce.
“All the same, I'd rather bite my own tongue out than fail in respect toward the sainted man you hold in such high regard,” he wrote at the end. Alyosha found little comfort in the letter.

title: I. They Arrive At The Monastery
paragraphs: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The meeting with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors didn't attend the service, but arrived just as it was ending. First, an elegant open carriage, drawn by two fine horses, pulled up carrying Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. This young man was preparing to enter university. Miüsov, with whom he was staying at the time, was trying to talk him into going abroad to study at Zurich or Jena. The young man was still undecided. He was pensive and absent-minded. He was nice-looking, sturdily built, and rather tall. There was an odd fixed quality to his gaze at times. Like all very absent-minded people, he'd sometimes stare straight at someone without actually seeing them. He was quiet and rather awkward, but sometimes, alone with someone, he'd turn talkative and animated, laughing at anything or nothing at all. But his liveliness would vanish as quickly as it appeared. He was always dressed well, even elaborately; he already had some money of his own, with expectations of a good deal more. He was a friend of Alyosha's.

In an ancient, jolting but roomy hired carriage, drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses, a good way behind Miüsov's, came Fyodor Pavlovitch with his son Ivan. Dmitri was late, though he'd been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriages at the hotel, outside the grounds, and walked to the monastery gates on foot. Except for Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of the party had ever seen the monastery before, and Miüsov had probably not set foot in a church in thirty years. He looked around with curiosity, along with a certain studied ease. But apart from the church and the outbuildings—ordinary enough in themselves—he found nothing of interest inside the monastery grounds. The last worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded, crossing themselves. Among the humbler people were a few of higher rank—two or three ladies and a very old general, all staying at the hotel. Our visitors were immediately surrounded by beggars, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov, who took a ten-copeck piece from his purse and, nervous and flustered—God knows why—hurriedly handed it to an old woman, saying, “Share it out equally.” None of his companions made any remark about it, so he had no real reason to be embarrassed, but, noticing this, he was even more thrown off.

It was odd that their arrival didn't seem to have been expected, and that they weren't received with any particular honor, even though one of them had recently made a donation of a thousand roubles, while another was an extremely wealthy, highly cultured landowner on whom, in a sense, the whole monastery depended, since a ruling in his lawsuit could put their fishing rights in his hands at any moment. Yet no official of the monastery came out to meet them.

Miüsov glanced absently at the tombstones around the church, and was on the verge of remarking that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right to lie in this “holy place,” but held his tongue. His liberal irony was rapidly curdling into something closer to anger.
“Who the devil is there to ask, in this idiotic place? We need to find out, time's getting on,” he muttered, as though talking to himself.

All at once a bald, elderly man with fawning little eyes came up, wearing a long summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself with a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He at once got wind of our visitors' difficulty.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, off by itself, four hundred paces from the monastery, on the other side of the copse.”
“I know it's the other side of the copse,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but we don't remember the way. It's been a long time since we were here.”
“This way, through this gate, straight across the copse… the copse. Come with me, won't you? I'll show you. I have to go… I'm going myself. This way, this way.”

They came out through the gate and turned toward the copse. Maximov, a man of sixty, ran rather than walked, turning sideways to stare at them all with an almost incredible degree of nervous curiosity, his eyes seeming to bulge out of his head.

“You see, we've come to the elder on business of our own,” Miüsov observed sternly. “That personage has granted us an audience, so to speak, and so, though we thank you for showing us the way, we can't ask you to come along with us.”
“I've already been there. I've been already; _un chevalier parfait_,” and Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.
“Who's a _chevalier_?” asked Miüsov.
“The elder, the splendid elder, the elder! The honor and glory of the monastery. Zossima. What an elder!”
But his rambling chatter was cut off by a very pale, wan-looking monk of medium height, wearing a monk's cap, who caught up with them. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
The monk, with an extremely courteous, deep bow, announced:
“The Father Superior invites all of you, gentlemen, to dine with him after your visit to the hermitage. At one o'clock, no later.” And to Maximov: “And you as well.”

“That I certainly will, without fail,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, hugely pleased by the invitation. “And, believe me, we've all given our word to behave ourselves here… And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go too?”
“Yes, of course. What did I come for, if not to study every custom here? The only thing standing in my way is your company…”
“Yes—Dmitri Fyodorovitch doesn't exist yet.”
“It'd be a capital thing if he never turned up at all. Do you suppose I enjoy any of this, and in your company besides? So, we'll come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior,” he said to the monk.
“No, it's my duty now to take you to the elder,” the monk answered.
“If that's so, I'll go straight to the Father Superior—straight to the Father Superior,” babbled Maximov.
“The Father Superior is occupied just now. But as you like—” the monk hesitated.
“Impertinent old man!” Miüsov said aloud, while Maximov ran back toward the monastery.
“He's like von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that all you can think of?… How on earth is he like von Sohn? Have you even seen von Sohn?”
“I've seen his portrait. It's not the features exactly, but something indefinable. He's a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy.”

“Ah, I daresay you're a connoisseur in that line. But look here, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you said just now we'd given our word to behave. Remember it. I'd advise you to control yourself. If you start clowning I don't intend to be associated with you here… You see what kind of man he is”—he turned to the monk—“I'm afraid to be seen among decent people with him.” A faint smile, not without a certain slyness, crossed the monk's pale, bloodless lips, but he made no reply, and clearly kept silent out of a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned more deeply than ever.
“Oh, devil take the lot of them—an outward show built up over centuries, and nothing underneath but charlatanism and nonsense,” flashed through Miüsov's mind.
“Here's the hermitage. We've arrived,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “The gates are shut.”
And he crossed himself repeatedly before the saints painted above and along the sides of the gates.

“When in Rome, do as the Romans do. Here in this hermitage there are twenty-five saints saving their souls. They look each other over and eat cabbage. And not one woman sets foot through this gate. That's the remarkable thing. And it really is so. But I did hear the elder receives ladies,” he added suddenly to the monk.

“Women of the common people are here too now, lying in the portico, waiting. But for ladies of higher rank, two rooms have been built adjoining the portico, outside the walls—you can see the windows there—and the elder goes out to them by an inner passage when he's well enough. They always stay outside the walls. There's a lady from Kharkov, Madame Hohlakov, waiting there now with her sick daughter. He's probably promised to come out to her, though lately he's been so weak he's barely shown himself even to the common people.”

“So there are loopholes, after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don't imagine, holy father, that I mean any harm by it. But did you know that on Athos, not only are women's visits forbidden—no creature of the female sex is allowed at all, not hens, not turkey-hens, not cows.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you, I'll turn around and leave you here. They'll throw you out the moment I'm gone.”
“But I'm not bothering you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he cried suddenly, stepping inside the grounds, “what a vale of roses they live in!”

Though there were no roses at that season, there were plenty of rare, beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was room for them, clearly tended by a skilled hand; there were flower beds around the church and between the graves, and the one-story wooden house where the elder lived was likewise surrounded with flowers.

“And was it like this in the time of the last elder, Varsonofy? He had no use for that kind of elegance. They say he used to jump up and thrash even the ladies with a stick,” Fyodor Pavlovitch remarked, climbing the steps.

“The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a lot of what's said is nonsense. He never thrashed anyone,” the monk answered. “Now, gentlemen, if you'll wait a moment, I'll go announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time—our agreement, do you hear? Behave yourself or I'll make you pay for it!” Miüsov managed to mutter again.

“I can't think why you're so worked up,” Fyodor Pavlovitch observed sarcastically. “Worried about your sins? They say he can tell what someone's come about just from their eyes. And what a lot of stock you put in their opinion, you—a Parisian, and so advanced! I'm amazed at you.”
But Miüsov had no time to answer this jab. They were asked to come in. He walked in, somewhat irritated.
“Now I know myself—I'm annoyed, I'll lose my temper and start a quarrel—and lower myself and my principles along with it,” he thought.

title: II. The Old Buffoon
paragraphs: They entered the room at almost the same moment the elder came in from his bedroom. Already waiting in the cell for him were two monks of the hermitage—one the Father Librarian, the other Father Païssy, a very learned man, so they said, in poor health though not old. There was also a tall young man of about twenty-two standing in the corner throughout the whole visit, wearing ordinary dress, with a broad, fresh face and clever, watchful, narrow brown eyes. He was a divinity student living under the monastery's protection. His expression was one of unquestioning yet self-respecting reverence. Being in a subordinate, dependent position, and thus not on an equal footing with the guests, he didn't greet them with a bow.
