Father Zossima was accompanied by a novice, and by Alyosha. The two monks rose and greeted him with a very deep bow, touching the ground with their fingers, then kissed his hand. Blessing them, the elder returned as deep a bow, and asked their blessing in turn. The whole ritual was performed with great seriousness, and with real feeling, not like some routine formality. But Miüsov got the impression it was all done with deliberate theatricality. He stood at the front of the other visitors. Out of simple politeness—he'd thought this over the night before, since it was the local custom—he ought to have gone up to receive the elder's blessing, even without kissing his hand. But watching all this bowing and hand-kissing among the monks, he instantly changed his mind. With dignified gravity he made a rather stiff, conventional bow, and stepped back to a chair. Fyodor Pavlovitch did exactly the same, aping Miüsov like a monkey. Ivan bowed with great dignity and courtesy, but kept his own hands at his sides, while Kalganov was so flustered he didn't bow at all. The elder let his raised hand drop from its blessing, and, bowing to them once more, invited them all to sit. The blood rushed to Alyosha's cheeks. He was ashamed. His forebodings were coming true.

Father Zossima sat down on a very old-fashioned mahogany sofa, upholstered in leather, and seated his visitors in a row along the opposite wall, on four mahogany chairs covered in worn black leather. The monks sat, one by the door, the other by the window. The divinity student, the novice, and Alyosha remained standing. The cell was not very large and had a faded look to it. It held nothing but the barest necessary furniture, of coarse, cheap quality. There were two pots of flowers in the window, and a number of holy images in the corner. Before one huge, ancient icon of the Virgin, a lamp was burning. Near it stood two other icons in gleaming settings, and beside them carved cherubim, porcelain eggs, an ivory Catholic crucifix with a Mater Dolorosa embracing it, and several foreign engravings by the great Italian masters of past centuries. Right next to these costly, artistic engravings hung several of the crudest Russian prints of saints and martyrs, the kind sold for a few kopecks at every fair. On the other walls hung portraits of Russian bishops, past and present.

Miüsov took a quick glance around at all these “conventional” surroundings and fixed an intent look on the elder. He thought highly of his own perceptiveness, an excusable weakness in a man of fifty, at an age when a clever man of the world with an established position can hardly help taking himself rather seriously. At first glance he didn't like Zossima. There was, in fact, something in the elder's face that many people besides Miüsov might not have liked. He was a short, bent little man with very weak legs, and though he was only sixty-five, he looked at least ten years older. His face was very thin and covered with a network of fine wrinkles, especially numerous around his eyes, which were small, pale, quick, and shone like two bright points. He had a scattering of gray hair at his temples. His small, pointed beard was sparse, and his lips, which smiled often, were thin as two threads. His nose wasn't long, but sharp, like a bird's beak.
“A malicious soul, by all appearances, full of petty pride,” thought Miüsov. He felt thoroughly dissatisfied with his own position there.
A cheap little clock on the wall struck twelve in a hurry, and it served to break the ice for conversation.

“Right on time,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but no sign of my son Dmitri. I apologize for him, holy elder!” (Alyosha flinched all over at “holy elder.”) “I'm always punctual myself, minute for minute, remembering that punctuality is the courtesy of kings…”
“But you're not a king, whatever else you are,” Miüsov muttered, losing his composure at once.

“Yes, that's true. I'm no king—and, would you believe it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I knew that myself. But there! I always say the wrong thing. Your reverence,” he cried, with sudden pathos, “you're looking at a buffoon in dead earnest! I introduce myself as one. It's an old habit, alas! And if I sometimes talk nonsense out of turn, it's with a purpose—to amuse people, to make myself agreeable. One has to be agreeable, doesn't one? I was, seven years ago, in a little town where I had some business, and I made friends with a few merchants there. We went to see the chief of police, because we had business with him and wanted to invite him to dinner. He was a tall, fat, fair-haired, sullen man—the most dangerous type in these matters. It's their liver, you know. I went straight up to him, and with the ease of a man of the world, I said, 'Mr. Ispravnik,' I said, 'do be our Napravnik.' 'What do you mean by Napravnik?' he says. I could tell, in half a second, that it had fallen flat. He just stood there, glum. 'I meant it as a joke,' I said, 'since Mr. Napravnik is our famous Russian orchestra conductor, and what we need for the harmony of our little venture is exactly someone of that kind.' And I explained my little comparison quite reasonably, didn't I? 'Excuse me,' he says, 'I am an Ispravnik, and I do not permit puns to be made on my title.' And he turned and walked off. I went after him, shouting, 'Yes, yes, you're an Ispravnik, not a Napravnik.' 'No,' he said, 'since you called me a Napravnik, that's what I am now.' And would you believe it, it ruined our whole piece of business! And I'm always like that—always. Forever wounding myself with my own politeness. Once, years ago, I told an influential man, 'Your wife is a ticklish lady'—meaning it honorably, about her moral qualities, so to speak. But he asked me, 'What, have you been tickling her?' I'd meant to be polite, so I couldn't help saying, 'Yes'—and he gave me a proper tickling right there on the spot. Though that was so long ago I'm not ashamed to tell the story now. I'm always injuring myself like that.”
“You're doing it right now,” Miüsov muttered, with disgust.
Father Zossima studied them both in silence.

“Am I? Would you believe it, I was aware of that too, Pyotr Alexandrovitch—and let me tell you, I actually foresaw it the moment I opened my mouth. And do you know, I even foresaw that you'd be the first one to point it out. The instant I see a joke isn't landing, your reverence, both my cheeks feel as though they're being dragged down toward my jaw, almost cramping. That's been true since I was young, back when I had to make jokes for my supper in noblemen's houses. I'm an incurable buffoon, and have been since birth, your reverence—it's practically a mania in me. I daresay there's a devil in me. But only a small one. A more serious devil would have picked a better lodging. Though not your soul, Pyotr Alexandrovitch—you're not much of a lodging either. But I do believe—I believe in God, though I've had my doubts lately. But right now I'm sitting here waiting for words of wisdom. I'm like the philosopher Diderot, your reverence. Did you ever hear, most holy Father, how Diderot went to call on Metropolitan Platon, in the time of Empress Catherine? He walked in and said flat out, 'There is no God.' To which the great bishop raised a finger and answered, 'The fool hath said in his heart there is no God.' And Diderot fell at his feet on the spot. 'I believe,' he cried, 'and I will be baptized.' And so he was. Princess Dashkov stood as his godmother, and Potyomkin his godfather.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is unbearable! You know perfectly well you're lying, and that stupid story isn't true. Why do you keep playing the fool?” Miüsov cried, his voice shaking.

“I suspected all my life it wasn't true,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, with total conviction. “But I'll tell you the whole truth, gentlemen. Great elder! Forgive me—the bit about Diderot's baptism I made up just now, on the spot. I'd never thought of it before. I made it up for a bit of extra spice. I play the fool, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to make myself agreeable. Though honestly I sometimes don't know myself what I do it for. As for Diderot, I heard the 'fool hath said in his heart' part a good twenty times from the local gentry when I was young. I heard your own aunt tell the story, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. They all believe, to this day, that the infidel Diderot came to argue about God with Metropolitan Platon…”
Miüsov got to his feet, forgetting himself in his impatience. He was furious, and painfully aware of looking ridiculous.

What was happening in the cell was, in truth, unbelievable. For forty or fifty years, going back to the time of the earlier elders, no visitor had ever entered that cell without a feeling of the deepest reverence. Almost everyone admitted there felt that a great honor was being shown him. Many stayed on their knees the entire visit. Among those visitors had been men of high rank and great learning, some even freethinkers, drawn by curiosity, and all of them without exception had shown the deepest reverence and delicacy, since here there was no question of money, only, on one side, love and kindness, and on the other, penitence and an eager desire to resolve some spiritual crisis or problem. So this kind of buffoonery left the onlookers stunned and bewildered—or at least some of them. The monks, their faces unchanged, waited with grave attention to hear what the elder would say, but seemed on the verge of standing up, like Miüsov. Alyosha stood with his head hanging, on the point of tears. What struck him as strangest of all was that his brother Ivan, on whom alone he'd pinned his hopes, and who alone had enough influence over their father to stop him, now sat there quite unmoved, eyes lowered, apparently waiting with interest to see how it would end, as if he had nothing to do with any of it. Alyosha didn't dare look at Rakitin, the divinity student, whom he knew almost intimately. He alone in the monastery knew what Rakitin was thinking.

“Forgive me,” Miüsov began, addressing Father Zossima, “for perhaps seeming to take part in this shameful farce. I made the mistake of thinking that even a man like Fyodor Pavlovitch would understand what's owed on a visit to so honored a person. I didn't expect I'd have to apologize simply for having come here with him…”
Pyotr Alexandrovitch could say no more, and was about to leave the room, overwhelmed with embarrassment.

“Don't distress yourself, I beg you.” The elder rose to his feeble legs, and, taking Pyotr Alexandrovitch by both hands, made him sit back down. “I beg you not to trouble yourself. I ask you especially to be my guest.” And with a bow he went back and sat down again on his little sofa.
“Great elder, speak! Do I trouble you with my liveliness?” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly cried, gripping the arms of his chair with both hands as though ready to leap up if the answer were unfavorable.

“I earnestly beg you too not to disturb yourself, and not to feel uneasy,” the elder said, with weight. “Don't trouble yourself. Make yourself entirely at home. And, above all, don't be so ashamed of yourself—that's the root of all this.”

“Entirely at home? My natural self? Oh, that's far too generous, but I accept it with grateful joy. You know, blessed Father, you'd better not invite me to be my natural self. Don't risk it… I won't go that far myself. I warn you, for your own sake. Well, the rest is still wrapped in the fog of uncertainty, though there are people who'd be glad to describe me for you. I mean that for you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. But as for you, holy man, let me tell you—I'm brimming over with rapture.”

He stood up, and, throwing up his hands, declaimed: “Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck—the paps especially. When you said just now, 'Don't be so ashamed of yourself, for that's the root of it all,' you pierced right through me with that remark, you read me to the core. Really, whenever I meet people I feel I'm lower than all of them, and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say to myself, 'Let me really play the buffoon, then. I'm not afraid of your opinion, because every one of you is worse than I am.' That's why I'm a buffoon. It's out of shame, great elder—out of shame; it's pure oversensitivity that makes me rowdy. If I'd only ever been sure that everyone would take me for the kindest, wisest of men, oh Lord, what a good man I'd have turned out to be! Teacher!”—he suddenly dropped to his knees—“what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
Even now it was hard to say whether he was joking or genuinely moved.
Father Zossima raised his eyes, looked at him, and said with a smile:

“You've known for a long time what you must do. You've sense enough for that: don't give way to drunkenness and loose talk; don't give way to sensual lust; and above all, to the love of money. And close your taverns. If you can't close them all, at least two or three. And, above all—don't lie.”
“You mean about Diderot?”

“No, not about Diderot. Above all, don't lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself, and listens to his own lie, ends up unable to tell truth from falsehood, in himself or around him, and so he loses respect for himself and for others. And having no respect, he stops loving, and, to occupy and distract himself without love, he gives himself over to passions and coarse pleasures, and sinks into pure bestiality in his vices—all from constant lying, to other people and to himself. The man who lies to himself is the one most easily offended of all. You know, it's sometimes quite pleasant to take offense, isn't it? A man may know perfectly well that no one has insulted him, but that he's invented the insult himself, lied about it and exaggerated it to make it more picturesque, seized on some word and made a mountain out of a molehill—he knows that himself, and yet he'll be the first to take offense, and revel in his resentment until he feels real pleasure in it, until it turns into genuine vindictiveness. But get up, sit down, please. All this, too, is a kind of deceitful posturing…”
“Blessed man! Give me your hand to kiss.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch sprang up and planted a quick kiss on the elder's thin hand. “It is, it's pleasant to take offense. You put that so well—I've never heard it put that way before. Yes, I've spent my whole life taking offense, to please myself, taking offense on aesthetic grounds, because it's not so much pleasant as distinguished, sometimes, to be insulted—that part you'd forgotten, great elder, it's distinguished! I'll make a note of that. But I've been lying—lying, positively, my whole life long, every day and every hour of it. Truly, I am a lie, and the father of lies. Though actually I don't think I'm the father of lies. I'm getting my texts mixed up. Say the son of lies instead, that'll do well enough. Only… my angel… I may occasionally bring up Diderot! Diderot won't do any harm, though sometimes a single word can. Great elder, by the way, I nearly forgot—though I've meant for two years now to come here on purpose to ask and find out something. Only tell Pyotr Alexandrovitch not to interrupt me. Here's my question: is it true, great Father, that somewhere in the _Lives of the Saints_ there's a story of a holy martyr who, when his head was finally cut off, stood up, picked up his own head, and, 'courteously kissing it,' walked a long way carrying it in his hands? Is that true or not, honored Father?”
“No, it's not true,” said the elder.
“There's nothing of the kind in any of the lives of the saints. Which saint are you talking about?” asked the Father Librarian.

“I don't know which saint. I don't know, I can't say. I was misled. I was told the story. I'd heard it—and do you know who told it to me? Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov here, who was so angry a minute ago about Diderot. He's the one who told the story.”
“I never told you any such thing. I don't even talk to you.”

“It's true you didn't tell it to me directly, but you told it while I was present. It was three years ago. I mention it because that ridiculous story shook my faith, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You had no idea you'd done it, but I went home with my faith shaken, and it's only gotten more shaken ever since. Yes, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you were the cause of a great fall. That was no Diderot!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch had worked himself up into quite a pathetic state, though by now it was perfectly clear to everyone he was playing a part again. Still, Miüsov was stung by the remark.

“What nonsense—it's all nonsense,” he muttered. “I may well have told it, at some point or other… but not to you. It was told to me. I heard it in Paris, from a Frenchman. He told me it was read out at our mass, from the _Lives of the Saints_… he was a very learned man who'd made a special study of Russian statistics, and had lived a long time in Russia… I haven't read the _Lives of the Saints_ myself, and I don't intend to… all sorts of things get said over dinner—we were dining at the time.”
“Yes, you were dining then, and that's how I lost my faith!” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, mimicking him.
“What do I care about your faith?” Miüsov was on the verge of shouting, but caught himself, and said instead, with contempt, “You defile everything you touch.”

The elder suddenly rose from his seat. “Excuse me, gentlemen, for leaving you a few minutes,” he said, addressing all his guests. “I have visitors waiting for me who arrived before you did. But don't you go on telling lies, all the same,” he added, turning to Fyodor Pavlovitch with a good-humored expression. He left the cell. Alyosha and the novice rushed to help him down the steps. Alyosha was breathless: he was glad to get away, but glad too that the elder was in good humor and not offended. Father Zossima was heading toward the portico to bless the people waiting for him there. But Fyodor Pavlovitch insisted on stopping him at the door of the cell.

“Blessed man!” he cried, with feeling. “Let me kiss your hand once more. Yes, with you I could still talk—I could still get along. Do you think I'm always lying and clowning around like this? Believe me, I've been putting on this whole act just to test you. I've been trying you out this whole time to see whether I could get along with you. Is there room for my humility next to your pride? I'm ready to give you a testimonial saying one can get along with you! But now I'll be quiet; I'll hold my tongue the rest of the time. I'll sit in a chair and say nothing. Now it's your turn to speak, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You're the main person left now—for ten minutes.”

title: III. Peasant Women Who Have Faith
paragraphs: Below, at the wooden portico built onto the outer wall of the enclosure, a crowd of about twenty peasant women had gathered. They'd been told the elder would finally be coming out, and had assembled in anticipation. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, had also come out onto the portico to wait for the elder, though in a separate section set aside for women of rank.

Madame Hohlakov was a wealthy woman, still young and attractive, always dressed with taste. She was somewhat pale, with lively black eyes. She was no more than thirty-three, and had been a widow for five years. Her daughter, a girl of fourteen, was partly paralyzed. The poor child hadn't been able to walk for the past six months, and was wheeled around in a long reclining chair. She had a charming little face, thin from illness but full of good humor. There was a gleam of mischief in her big dark eyes with their long lashes. Her mother had been meaning to take her abroad since spring, but they'd been held up all summer by business connected with their estate. They'd been staying a week in our town, having come mostly on business rather than for devotion, but had already visited Father Zossima once, three days before. Though they knew the elder scarcely saw anyone now, they'd suddenly turned up again, urgently begging for “the happiness of looking once more on the great healer.”

The mother sat on a chair beside her daughter's invalid carriage, and two paces off stood an old monk—not from our monastery, but a visitor from an obscure religious house in the far north. He too had come seeking the elder's blessing.

But Father Zossima, on entering the portico, went first straight to the peasants crowded at the foot of the three steps leading up into it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women pressing around him. One deranged woman was led up to him. The moment she caught sight of the elder she began shrieking and writhing as though in labor. Laying the stole on her forehead, he read a short prayer over her, and she was at once calmed and quieted.

I don't know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in the villages and monasteries. They'd be brought to mass, and would squeal and bark like dogs, loud enough to be heard through the whole church. But the moment the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” would stop at once, and the sick women would always be soothed for a while. As a child I found this deeply striking and astonishing, but I heard from country neighbors and from my town teachers that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that it could always be cured with a bit of proper strictness; various anecdotes were told to back this up. But later on I learned, to my surprise, from medical specialists that there's nothing fake about it, that it's a terrible illness women are subject to, especially common here in Russia, and that it comes from the hard lot of peasant women. It's a disease, I was told, arising from exhausting labor taken up too soon after difficult, unassisted childbirths, and from the hopeless misery, the beatings, and so on, which some women simply couldn't bear as well as others could. The strange, instant healing of the frantic, struggling woman the moment she was brought before the holy sacrament, which had been explained to me as a matter of malingering and clerical trickery, most likely arose in the most natural way possible. Both the women supporting her and the invalid herself believed, without question, as an absolute truth, that the evil spirit possessing her couldn't hold out if the sick woman were brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. And so, in a nervous, psychologically disturbed woman, a kind of convulsion of the whole body would take place—and was bound to take place—at the moment of bowing down before the sacrament, stirred up by the expectation of a miraculous cure and the absolute belief that it would happen; and it did happen, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, the instant the elder touched the sick woman with his stole.
Many of the women in the crowd were moved to tears of rapture by the moment; some strained to kiss the hem of his robe, others cried out in a kind of sing-song wail.
He blessed them all and spoke with some of them. He already knew the “possessed” woman. She came from a village only four miles from the monastery, and had been brought to him before.

“But here's one from far away.” He pointed to a woman, not old, but very thin and worn, her face not just sunburnt but nearly blackened by exposure. She was on her knees, gazing at the elder with a fixed stare—there was something almost frenzied in her eyes.

“From far away, Father, from far away! From two hundred miles off. From far away, Father, from far away!” the woman began in a sing-song voice, as if chanting a dirge, swaying her head from side to side, her cheek resting in her hand.

There's a silent, long-suffering grief you find among the peasantry. It draws inward and stays still. But there's also a grief that breaks loose, and from that moment bursts into tears and finds its outlet in wailing. This is especially common among women. But it's no lighter a grief than the silent kind. Wailing brings comfort only by tearing the heart open further still. Grief of that kind doesn't want to be consoled. It feeds on the very sense of its own hopelessness. The wailing springs only from a constant craving to reopen the wound.
“You're of the tradesman class?” said Father Zossima, looking at her curiously.

“Townsfolk we are, Father, townsfolk. Though we're peasants at heart even living in town. I've come to see you, oh Father! We heard about you, Father, we heard about you. I've buried my little son, and I've come on a pilgrimage. I've been to three monasteries, but they told me, 'Go, Nastasya, go to him'—meaning you. I've come; I was at the service yesterday, and today I've come to you.”
“What are you weeping for?”

“It's my little son I'm grieving for, Father. He was three years old—three years all but three months. I'm in agony over my boy, Father, over my little boy. He was the last one I had left. There were four of us, my Nikita and I, and now we've no children—our dear ones are all gone. I buried the first three without grieving so terribly, but this last one I can't forget. He's always standing before me. He never leaves me. He's withered my heart. I look at his little clothes, his little shirt, his little boots, and I wail. I lay out everything that's left of him, all his little things. I look at them and wail. I say to Nikita, my husband, 'Let me go on a pilgrimage, master.' He's a driver. We're not poor people, Father, not poor—he drives his own horse. It's all ours, the horse and the carriage. And what good is any of it to us now? My Nikita's taken to drinking while I'm away. He's sure to. It's always been that way before. The moment I turn my back he gives in to it. But now I don't think about him at all. It's three months since I left home. I've forgotten him. I've forgotten everything. I don't want to remember. And what would our life together even be now? I'm done with him, I'm done. I'm done with all of them. I don't want to look at my house or my belongings. I don't want to see anything at all!”

“Listen, mother,” said the elder. “Once, in olden times, a holy saint saw in the Temple a mother like you, weeping for her little one, her only child, whom God had taken. 'Knowest thou not,' the saint said to her, 'how bold these little ones are before the throne of God? Truly, there are none bolder than they in the Kingdom of Heaven. “Thou didst give us life, O Lord,” they say, “and scarcely had we looked upon it when Thou didst take it back again.” And they ask, and ask so boldly, that God gives them at once the rank of angels.' 'Therefore,' the saint said, 'thou too, O mother, rejoice and weep not, for thy little son is with the Lord, among the fellowship of angels.' That's what the saint said to the weeping mother, long ago. He was a great saint, and he wouldn't have spoken falsely. So you too, mother, know that your little one is surely standing before the throne of God, rejoicing, happy, and praying to God for you—so weep not, but rejoice.”
The woman listened to him, her cheek still in her hand, eyes lowered. She sighed deeply.

“My Nikita tried to comfort me with those same words. 'Foolish woman,' he said, 'why do you weep? Our son is surely singing with the angels before God.' He says that to me, but he weeps himself. I see him cry, same as me. 'I know, Nikita,' I say. 'Where else could he be, if not with the Lord God? Only, here with us, he isn't as he used to be, sitting beside us the way he used to.' And if only I could look at him one little time—if only I could peek at him for one little moment, without going up to him, without speaking, if I could just hide in a corner and see him for one little minute, hear him playing in the yard, calling out in his little voice, 'Mammy, where are you?' If only I could hear him pattering with his little feet across the room just once, only once—because so often, so often, I remember how he used to run to me, shouting and laughing—if I could only hear his little feet I'd know it was him! But he's gone, Father, he's gone, and I'll never hear him again. Here's his little sash, but him I'll never see or hear now.”

She pulled out from inside her dress her boy's little embroidered sash, and the moment she looked at it she began shaking with sobs, covering her eyes with her fingers as the tears poured through them in a sudden stream.

“This is Rachel of old,” said the elder, “weeping for her children, and refusing comfort because they are no more. That is the fate set on earth for mothers like you. Do not be comforted. Comfort isn't what you need. Weep, and do not be consoled—only weep. Just remember, every time you weep, that your little son is one of the angels of God now, that he looks down at you from there and sees you, and rejoices in your tears, and points them out to the Lord God; and for a long while yet you'll carry this great mother's grief. But in the end it will turn into quiet joy, and your bitter tears will become only tears of tender sorrow, the kind that purifies the heart and frees it from sin. And I'll pray for the peace of your child's soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”
“A sweet name. After Alexey, the man of God?”
“Yes, Father.”

“What a saint he was! I'll remember him, mother, and your grief, in my prayers—and I'll pray for your husband's health too. It's a sin for you to leave him. Your little one will see from heaven that you've abandoned his father, and he'll weep over you. Why trouble his happiness? He is alive—for the soul lives forever—and though he's not in the house, he's near you, unseen. How could he come into the house if you say the house is hateful to you? Who would he go to, if he can't find his father and mother together? He comes to you in dreams now, and you grieve. But then he'll send you gentle dreams instead. Go to your husband, mother; go this very day.”

“I'll go, Father, at your word. I'll go. You've gone straight to my heart. My Nikita, my Nikita, you're waiting for me,” the woman began in her sing-song voice; but the elder had already turned away, to a very old woman dressed like a town-dweller, not a pilgrim. Her eyes showed she'd come with a purpose, to say something in particular. She said she was the widow of a non-commissioned officer, and lived close by in town. Her son Vasenka was in the commissariat service, and had gone off to Irkutsk in Siberia. He'd written twice from there, but now a year had passed without a letter. She'd tried to make inquiries about him, but didn't know the right place to ask.

“Just the other day Stepanida Ilyinishna—she's a rich merchant's wife—said to me, 'You go, Prohorovna, and have your son's name put down for prayer at church, and pray for the peace of his soul as if he were dead. His soul will be troubled,' she said, 'and he'll write you a letter.' And Stepanida Ilyinishna told me it was a sure thing, tried many times before. Only I'm not certain… Oh, you, our light—is it true, or false, and would it even be right to do?”

“Don't even think of it. It's shameful to ask such a question. How could one possibly pray for the peace of a living soul? And his own mother, at that! It's a great sin, close to sorcery. It's only forgiven you because of your ignorance. Better to pray to the Queen of Heaven, our swift defender and helper, for his good health, and to ask her forgiveness for your error. And I'll tell you one more thing, Prohorovna: either your son will come back to you soon, or he'll be sure to send a letter. Go, and be at peace from now on. Your son is alive, I tell you.”
“Dear Father, God reward you, our benefactor, who prays for all of us and for our sins!”

But the elder had already noticed, in the crowd, two burning eyes fixed on him. An exhausted, consumptive-looking, though still young peasant woman was gazing at him in silence. Her eyes pleaded, but she seemed afraid to come closer.
“What is it, my child?”
“Absolve my soul, Father,” she said softly, and slowly sank to her knees and bowed down at his feet. “I have sinned, Father. I am afraid of my sin.”
The elder sat down on the lower step. The woman crept closer to him, still on her knees.

“I have been a widow these three years,” she began in a half-whisper, with a kind of shudder. “My life with my husband was hard. He was an old man. He used to beat me cruelly. He fell ill; I looked at him and thought, if he got well, if he got up again, what then? And then the thought came to me—”
“Wait!” said the elder, and he brought his ear close to her lips.
The woman went on in a low whisper, so faint it was almost impossible to make out. She finished quickly.
“Three years ago?” asked the elder.
“Three years. At first I didn't think much about it, but now I've started to fall ill, and the thought won't leave me.”
“Have you come a long way?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you confessed it?”
“I have confessed it. Twice I've confessed it.”
“Have you been admitted to Communion?”
“Yes. I am afraid. I am afraid to die.”

“Fear nothing, and never be afraid; and don't fret. As long as your repentance doesn't fail, God will forgive everything. There is no sin, and there can be no sin on the whole earth, that the Lord will not forgive to the truly repentant! A man cannot commit a sin so great it would exhaust the infinite love of God. Can there even be a sin that could outstrip the love of God? Think only of repentance, of continual repentance—but let go of fear entirely. Believe that God loves you in a way you can't even conceive; that he loves you with your sin, in your sin. It's been said, of old, that there's more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ten righteous men. Go, and be not afraid. Don't turn bitter against people. Don't be angry when you're wronged. Forgive the dead man in your heart whatever wrong he did you. Be reconciled with him, truly. If you repent, you love. And if you love, you belong to God. All things are atoned for, all things are saved, by love. If I, a sinner just as you are, can be tender with you and pity you, how much more will God. Love is such a priceless treasure that you can redeem the whole world with it, and atone not only for your own sins, but for the sins of others too.”
He made the sign of the cross over her three times, took a small icon from around his own neck, and put it on her. She bowed all the way to the ground without a word.
He stood up, and looked cheerfully at a healthy peasant woman holding a tiny baby.
“From Vyshegorye, dear Father.”
“Five miles you've dragged yourself with the baby. What do you need?”

“I came to look at you. I've been to see you before—or have you forgotten? You've no great memory if you've forgotten me. They told us you were ill. Thinks I, I'll go see for myself. Well, now I see you, and you're not ill at all! You'll live another twenty years. God bless you! There's plenty praying for you—how could you fall ill?”
“Thank you for all of it, daughter.”

“By the way, I've got one thing to ask, not a big one. Here's sixty kopecks. Give it, dear Father, to someone poorer than me. I thought, as I was coming along, better to give it through you. You'll know who to give it to.”
“Thank you, my dear, thank you! You're a good woman. I love you. I'll certainly see to it. Is that your little girl?”
“My little girl, Father, Lizaveta.”
“May the Lord bless you both, you and your little Lizaveta! You've gladdened my heart, mother. Farewell, dear children, farewell, dear ones.”
He blessed them all and bowed low to them.

title: IV. A Lady Of Little Faith
paragraphs: A visitor watching the scene of his conversation with the peasants and his blessing them shed silent tears, wiping them away with her handkerchief. She was a sentimental society lady, genuinely good-natured in many respects. When the elder finally came up to her, she greeted him with great enthusiasm.

“Ah, what I've been feeling, watching that touching scene!…” She couldn't go on, overcome with emotion. “Oh, I understand the people's love for you. I love the common people myself. I want to love them. And who couldn't love them—our splendid Russian people, so simple in their greatness!”
“How is your daughter's health? You wanted to speak with me again?”

“Oh, I've been begging for it so urgently, I've prayed for it! I was ready to fall on my knees and kneel for three days outside your windows until you let me in. We've come, great healer, to express our heartfelt gratitude. You have healed my Lise—healed her completely—simply by praying over her last Thursday and laying your hands on her. We've hurried here to kiss those hands, to pour out our feelings and our devotion.”
“What do you mean, healed? She's still lying in her chair.”

“But her night fevers stopped completely, ever since Thursday,” the lady said, with nervous haste. “And that's not all. Her legs are stronger. This morning she got up perfectly well; she'd slept all night. Look at her rosy cheeks, her bright eyes! She used to be crying constantly, but now she laughs, she's cheerful and happy. This morning she insisted I let her stand, and she stood for a whole minute without any support at all. She's wagering that in two weeks she'll be dancing a quadrille. I called in Dr. Herzenstube. He shrugged his shoulders and said, 'I'm amazed; I can make nothing of it.' And would you have us stay away, not come here to disturb you, not fly here to thank you? Lise, thank him—thank him!”

Lise's pretty, laughing little face suddenly turned serious. She raised herself as far as she could in her chair, looked at the elder, and clasped her hands before him—but couldn't restrain herself, and burst out laughing.
“It's at him,” she said, pointing at Alyosha, with childish annoyance at herself for not being able to stop laughing.
Anyone who'd looked at Alyosha, standing a step behind the elder, would have caught a quick flush crimsoning his cheeks in an instant. His eyes shone and he looked down.
“She has a message for you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How are you?” the mother went on, holding out an exquisitely gloved hand to Alyosha.
The elder turned and glanced attentively at Alyosha. The young man went closer to Lise, and, smiling in an oddly awkward way, held out his hand to her as well. Lise put on an important air.
“Katerina Ivanovna sent you this, through me.” She handed him a little note. “She particularly begs you to come and see her as soon as possible—that you won't fail her, that you'll be sure to come.”

“She's asking me to come see her? Me? What for?” Alyosha muttered, thoroughly astonished. His face at once looked anxious. “Oh, it's all to do with Dmitri Fyodorovitch—and what's happened lately,” the mother explained hurriedly. “Katerina Ivanovna has made up her mind, but she needs to see you about it… Why, exactly, I couldn't say. But she wants to see you right away. And of course you'll go to her. It's a Christian duty.”
“I've only met her once,” Alyosha protested, still just as puzzled.
“Oh, she's such an exalted, incomparable creature! If only for her suffering… Think what she's been through, what she's going through now! Think what awaits her! It's all terrible, terrible!”
“Very well, I'll come,” Alyosha decided, after quickly scanning the brief, cryptic note, which consisted of nothing but an urgent plea for him to come, with no explanation of any kind.

“Oh, how sweet and generous of you!” cried Lise, suddenly animated. “I told mama you'd be sure not to go. I said you were busy saving your soul. How splendid you are! I've always thought you were splendid. I'm so glad I can tell you so!”
“Lise!” her mother said sternly, though she smiled right after saying it.
“You've quite forgotten us, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said; “you never come to see us. And yet Lise has told me twice that she's never happy except with you.”

Alyosha raised his lowered eyes, flushed again, and again smiled without quite knowing why. But the elder was no longer watching him. He'd already begun talking with a monk who, as mentioned earlier, had been waiting by Lise's chair for his turn. He was evidently a monk of the humblest, peasant sort, narrow in outlook, but a true believer, and, in his own way, a stubborn one. He announced that he'd come from the far north, from Obdorsk, from Saint Sylvester, and belonged to a poor monastery of only ten monks. The elder gave him his blessing and invited him to visit his cell whenever he liked.
“How can you presume to do such things?” the monk asked suddenly, pointing solemnly, meaningfully, at Lise. He meant her “healing.”

“It's too soon, of course, to speak of that. Relief isn't the same as a full cure, and it can come from any number of causes. But if there has been any healing, it's by no power but God's will. It's all from God. Come visit me, Father,” he added to the monk. “I can't often see visitors. I'm ill, and I know my days are numbered.”
“Oh, no, no! God won't take you from us. You'll live a long, long time yet,” the lady cried. “And what's wrong with you? You look so well, so cheerful and happy.”

“I'm remarkably better today. But I know it's only for the moment. I understand my illness thoroughly now. If I seem so happy to you, you couldn't say anything that would please me more. For men were made for happiness, and anyone who is fully happy has the right to say to himself, 'I am doing God's will on earth.' All the righteous, all the saints, all the holy martyrs, were happy.”

“Oh, how you talk! What bold, lofty words!” the lady cried. “You seem to pierce right through with your words. And yet—happiness, happiness—where is it? Who can say of himself that he's happy? Oh, since you've been so good as to let us see you again today, let me tell you what I couldn't say last time, what I didn't dare say—everything I'm suffering, and have suffered for so long! I am suffering! Forgive me! I am suffering!”
And in a rush of fervent feeling she clasped her hands before him.
“From what, specifically?”
“I suffer… from a lack of faith.”
“A lack of faith in God?”

“Oh, no, no! I wouldn't even dare think that. But the life beyond—it's such a riddle! And no one, no one can solve it. Listen! You're a healer, you understand the human soul deeply, and of course I don't dare expect you to believe me completely, but I give you my word of honor that I'm not speaking lightly now. The thought of life beyond the grave drives me to anguish, to sheer terror. And I don't know who to turn to, and I've never dared, my whole life. And now I'm bold enough to ask you. Oh, God! What will you think of me now?”
She clasped her hands.
“Don't worry yourself over my opinion of you,” said the elder. “I fully believe your suffering is sincere.”

“Oh, how grateful I am to you! You see, I close my eyes and ask myself—if everyone has faith, where did it come from? And then people say it all comes from terror at the threatening forces of nature, and that none of it is real. And I say to myself, 'What if I've believed all my life, and when I come to die there's nothing but burdocks growing on my grave?' as I read in some author. It's terrible! How—how can I get my faith back? But I only ever believed as a small child, mechanically, without thinking about any of it. How, how is one to prove it? I've come now to lay my soul open before you, to ask you about it. If I let this chance slip, no one, for the rest of my life, will answer me. How can I prove it? How can I convince myself? Oh, how unhappy I am! I stand and look around me and see that hardly anyone else cares; no one troubles their head over it, and I'm the only one who can't bear it. It's deadly—deadly!”
“No doubt. But it can't be proven, though it can be made certain.”
“How?”

“Through the practice of active love. Strive to love your neighbor actively and tirelessly. The further you advance in love, the surer you'll grow of the reality of God, and of your soul's immortality. If you reach complete self-forgetfulness in loving your neighbor, then you'll believe beyond doubt, and no doubt will ever be able to enter your soul again. This has been tested. This much is certain.”

“Active love? There's another question—and what a question! You see, I love humanity so much that—would you believe it?—I often dream of giving up everything I have, leaving Lise, and becoming a sister of mercy. I close my eyes and think, and dream, and at that moment I feel strong enough to overcome any obstacle. No wounds, no festering sores, could frighten me at that moment. I'd bind them up and wash them with my own hands. I'd nurse the afflicted. I'd be ready to kiss such wounds.”
“That's a great deal, and it's well your mind runs to such dreams and not to others. Someday, without meaning to, you may do a genuine good deed.”

“Yes. But could I bear such a life for long?” the lady went on, still fervent, almost frantic. “That's the main question—that's my most tormenting question. I close my eyes and ask myself, 'Would you keep on that path for long? And if the patient whose wounds you're washing didn't meet you with gratitude, but tormented you with his whims, ignoring or belittling your charitable service, started abusing you, ordering you around rudely, complaining about you to the authorities above'—which happens often enough with people in great suffering—'what then? Would you go on loving, or not?' And you know, I came to the horrified conclusion that, if anything could dissolve my love for humanity, it would be ingratitude. In short, I'm a hired servant—I want my wages up front, that is, praise, love paid back for love. Otherwise I'm simply incapable of loving anyone.”
She was in a real fit of self-castigation, and, finishing, she gave the elder a look of defiant resolve.

“That's exactly the same story a doctor once told me,” the elder observed. “He was a man well on in years, and undoubtedly a clever one. He spoke as frankly as you do, though in jest—bitter jest. 'I love humanity,' he said, 'but I wonder at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love people in particular. In my dreams,' he said, 'I've often worked myself up into enthusiastic plans for serving humanity, and might genuinely have gone to my own crucifixion if it had suddenly been necessary; and yet I'm incapable of living in the same room with anyone for even two days, as I know from experience. The moment anyone comes near me, his personality gets in the way of my self-satisfaction and cramps my freedom. Within twenty-four hours I start to hate the best of men—one because he takes too long over dinner, another because he's got a cold and keeps blowing his nose. I turn hostile to people the moment they get close to me. But it's always worked out that the more I detest people individually, the more ardent my love for humanity as a whole becomes.'”
“But what's to be done? What can one do in such a case? Must one give up in despair?”

“No. It's enough that you're troubled by it. Do what you can, and it will be counted to you. A great deal has already been done in you, since you can look into yourself so deeply and sincerely. If you've been speaking to me this openly only to win my approval for your candor—as you just did—then of course you'll never get anywhere in achieving real love; it will all remain in the realm of dreams, and your whole life will slip past you like a phantom. In that case you'll naturally stop thinking about the life to come as well, and in the end you'll grow calmer, after a fashion, on your own.”

“You've crushed me! Only now, as you speak, do I understand that I really was only seeking your approval for my sincerity, when I told you I couldn't bear ingratitude. You've revealed me to myself. You've seen right through me and explained me to myself!”

“Are you speaking the truth? Well, now, after such a confession, I believe you're sincere, and good at heart. If you never reach happiness, always remember that you're on the right road, and try not to leave it. Above all, avoid falsehood—every kind of falsehood, especially falseness to yourself. Watch your own deceitfulness, and examine it every hour, every minute. Avoid being scornful, both of others and of yourself. Whatever seems bad to you within yourself will grow purer simply from the fact of your noticing it in yourself. Avoid fear too, though fear is really only the consequence of every kind of falsehood. Never let your own faintheartedness in the pursuit of love frighten you. Don't be too frightened, even, by your own bad actions. I'm sorry I can't say anything more comforting to you, because love in action is a harsh, dreadful thing next to love in dreams. Love in dreams craves quick action, swiftly carried out, and in full view of everyone. People will even give their lives, so long as the ordeal doesn't drag on, and is soon over, with everyone watching and applauding as if it were on a stage. But active love means labor and endurance, and, for some people, perhaps, an entire science of its own. But I'll tell you this: right when you see, with horror, that despite all your efforts you're getting farther from your goal instead of closer to it—right at that moment, I predict, you'll reach it, and see clearly the miraculous power of the Lord, who has been loving and secretly guiding you the whole time. Forgive me for not being able to stay with you longer. They're waiting for me. Good-bye.”
The lady was weeping.
“Lise, Lise! Bless her—bless her!” she cried, suddenly starting up.
“She doesn't deserve to be loved. I've seen her naughtiness the whole time,” the elder said, joking. “Why have you been laughing at Alexey?”

Lise had in fact spent the whole time mocking him. She'd noticed before that Alyosha was shy and tried not to look at her, and found this enormously funny. She'd been watching intently, waiting to catch his eye. Alyosha, unable to bear her relentless stare, was irresistibly, suddenly drawn to glance at her, and at once she smiled in triumph right in his face. Alyosha grew even more flustered and annoyed. Finally he turned away from her entirely, and hid behind the elder's back. A few minutes later, pulled by the same irresistible force, he turned again to see whether he was being watched or not, and found Lise nearly hanging out of her chair, peeping sideways at him, eagerly waiting for him to look. The instant she caught his eye, she laughed so hard the elder couldn't help saying, “Why do you tease him like that, naughty girl?”
Lise blushed, suddenly and quite unexpectedly. Her eyes flashed, and her face turned entirely serious. She started speaking quickly, nervously, in a warm, resentful voice:

“Why has he forgotten everything, then? He used to carry me around when I was little. We used to play together. He used to come and teach me to read, you know. Two years ago, when he went away, he said he'd never forget me, that we'd be friends forever, forever, forever! And now, all of a sudden, he's afraid of me. Am I going to eat him? Why doesn't he want to come near me? Why won't he talk? Why won't he come and see us? It's not that you won't allow him. We know he goes everywhere. It's not proper for me to invite him. He ought to have thought of it himself, if he hasn't forgotten me. No—now he's saving his soul! Why did you put that long robe on him? If he runs, he'll fall.”

And suddenly she buried her face in her hands and burst into irresistible, prolonged, nervous, silent laughter. The elder listened to her with a smile, and blessed her tenderly. As she kissed his hand she suddenly pressed it to her eyes and began to cry.
“Don't be angry with me. I'm silly and good for nothing… and maybe Alyosha's right, quite right, not wanting to come see such a ridiculous girl.”
“I'll certainly send him to you,” said the elder.

title: V. So Be It! So Be It!
paragraphs: The elder had been away from his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was past half-past twelve, but Dmitri, on whose account they'd all gathered there, still hadn't shown up. But he seemed almost forgotten, and when the elder came back into the cell, he found his guests deep in eager conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to join in too, apparently quite eagerly, but without much success there either. He was clearly on the sidelines, and his remarks were being brushed aside, which only sharpened his irritation. He'd had intellectual clashes with Ivan before, and couldn't stand a certain carelessness Ivan showed toward him.
“Up to now, at least, I've stood in the front ranks of everything progressive in Europe, and here the new generation simply ignores us,” he thought.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who'd given his word to sit still and keep quiet, had actually managed it for a while, but he watched his neighbor Miüsov with a sly little smile, plainly enjoying his discomfort. He'd been waiting a while to settle some old scores, and now he couldn't let the chance slip. Leaning over his shoulder, he started needling him again in a whisper.

“Why didn't you leave just now, after that 'courteously kissing' business? Why did you agree to stay in such unseemly company? Because you felt insulted, aggrieved, and stayed to vindicate yourself by showing off how clever you are. Now you won't leave until you've displayed your intellect for them.”
“You again?… On the contrary, I'm just about to leave.”
“You'll be the last, the very last one to go!” Fyodor Pavlovitch got in another jab, just as Father Zossima returned.

The discussion died down for a moment, but the elder, taking his old seat, looked around at them all as though warmly inviting them to continue. Alyosha, who knew every shade of his expression, saw that he was terribly exhausted and forcing himself to keep going. Lately he'd been prone to fainting fits from sheer weakness. His face had the pallor that always came before such attacks, and his lips were white. But he clearly didn't want to break up the gathering. He seemed to have some particular purpose of his own for keeping them there. What purpose? Alyosha watched him closely.

“We're discussing this gentleman's very interesting article,” said Father Iosif, the librarian, addressing the elder and indicating Ivan. “He raises a good deal that's new, but I think the argument cuts both ways. It's an article written in response to a book by a churchman on the question of ecclesiastical courts, and the scope of their jurisdiction.”
“I'm sorry I haven't read your article, but I've heard of it,” said the elder, looking closely and intently at Ivan.
“He takes a most interesting position,” the Father Librarian went on. “As far as Church jurisdiction goes, he seems entirely opposed to separating Church from State.”
“That's interesting. But in what sense?” Father Zossima asked Ivan.
Ivan finally answered him—not condescendingly, as Alyosha had feared, but with modesty and restraint, evidently with goodwill, and, it seemed, without the slightest ulterior motive.

“I start from the position that this mixing of elements—that is, of the essential principles of Church and State—will, of course, go on forever, despite the fact that the two simply cannot blend, and that mixing these elements can never lead to any consistent or even normal result, since there's a falsehood at the very foundation of it. Compromise between Church and State on questions like jurisdiction is, to my mind, impossible in any real sense. My clerical opponent maintains that the Church occupies a precise, well-defined place within the State. I maintain, on the contrary, that the Church ought to encompass the whole State, not merely occupy some corner of it—and if that's impossible for the time being, for whatever reason, then it ought, in truth, to be set up as the direct, principal aim of the future development of Christian society!”
“Perfectly true,” Father Païssy, the silent, learned monk, agreed with real fervor and conviction.
“Pure Ultramontanism!” cried Miüsov impatiently, crossing and re-crossing his legs.

“Well, we have no mountains,” cried Father Iosif, and, turning to the elder, went on: “Notice how he answers the following 'fundamental and essential' claims of his opponent—who is, you should note, a churchman himself. First, that 'no social organization can or should claim the power to dispose of the civic and political rights of its members.' Second, that 'criminal and civil jurisdiction should not belong to the Church, and is inconsistent with its nature, both as a divine institution and as an organization of men for religious ends.' And finally, third, that 'the Church is a kingdom not of this world.'”

“A most unworthy play on words, for a churchman!” Father Païssy couldn't stop himself from breaking in again. “I've read the book you're answering,” he added, turning to Ivan, “and I was astonished at the phrase 'the Church is a kingdom not of this world.' If it isn't of this world, then it can't exist on earth at all. In the Gospel, the words 'not of this world' aren't used in that sense. Playing games with such words is indefensible. Our Lord Jesus Christ came to establish the Church on earth. The Kingdom of Heaven, of course, is not of this world, but in Heaven—but it's only entered through the Church that's been founded and established here on earth. And so a frivolous play on words of that kind is unpardonable, and improper. The Church is, in truth, a kingdom, ordained to rule, and in the end must undoubtedly become the kingdom ruling over the whole earth. For that we have the divine promise.”
He stopped abruptly, as if checking himself. After listening attentively and respectfully, Ivan continued, still addressing the elder with perfect composure, and as before with ready warmth:

“The whole point of my article is that during the first three centuries, Christianity existed on earth only in the Church, and was nothing but the Church. When the pagan Roman Empire wished to become Christian, it inevitably happened that, in becoming Christian, it absorbed the Church but remained, in a great many of its functions, a pagan State still. In reality this was bound to happen. But Rome, as a State, held onto far too much of its pagan civilization and culture—in the very objects and founding principles of the State itself, for instance. The Christian Church, entering into the State, could of course surrender no part of its fundamental principles—the rock it stands on—and could pursue no aims other than those ordained and revealed by God himself, among them drawing the whole world, and so the ancient pagan State itself, into the Church. In that sense—that is, looking to the future—it isn't the Church that should seek out some defined place within the State, like 'every social organization,' or as 'an organization of men for religious purposes' (as my opponent calls the Church); rather, every earthly State should, in the end, be entirely transformed into the Church, and become nothing else but a Church, rejecting every aim incompatible with the Church's own. None of this would degrade the State in any way, or diminish its honor and glory as a great State, or the glory of its rulers—it would only turn it from a false, still-pagan, mistaken path onto the true, rightful one, the only path that leads to the eternal goal. That's why the author of _On the Foundations of Church Jurisdiction_ would have judged rightly, if, in setting out those foundations, he'd treated them as a temporary compromise, forced on us by our sinful, imperfect age. But the moment the author goes so far as to declare that the foundations he lays down now—some of which Father Iosif just listed—are the permanent, essential, eternal foundations, he's going directly against the Church and its sacred, eternal calling. That's the substance of my article.”

“In short,” Father Païssy began again, weighing each word, “according to certain theories—set out clearly enough in the nineteenth century—the Church ought to be transformed into the State, as though this would mark an advance from a lower form to a higher one, so that it disappears into the State, making room for science, for the spirit of the age, for civilization. And if the Church resists and refuses, some corner will be set aside for it within the State—and even that under supervision—and this will hold everywhere, in every modern European country. But Russian hopes and Russian thinking demand not that the Church pass, as from a lower into a higher type, into the State, but, on the contrary, that the State should end by being worthy to become nothing but the Church itself, and nothing else. So be it! So be it!”

“Well, I confess you've reassured me somewhat,” Miüsov said, smiling, crossing his legs again. “As far as I understand, then, the realization of such an ideal is infinitely remote—it waits on the second coming of Christ. That's your business. It's a lovely utopian dream of the abolition of war, diplomacy, banks, and so on—something in the fashion of socialism, really. But I thought all this was meant seriously, that the Church might, even now, be about to try criminals, and sentence them to flogging, prison, even death.”

“But if there were no court but the ecclesiastical one, the Church wouldn't, even now, sentence a criminal to prison or death. Crime, and how it's viewed, would inevitably change—not all at once, of course, but fairly soon,” Ivan replied calmly, without flinching.
“Are you serious?” Miüsov shot him a sharp look.

“If the Church took in everything, the Church would exclude all the criminal and the disobedient, rather than cutting off their heads,” Ivan went on. “I ask you—what would become of the excluded? He'd be cut off then not just from other men, as now, but from Christ himself. By his crime he'd have transgressed not only against men, but against the Church of Christ. That's already true now, strictly speaking, of course, but it's not clearly stated, and very, very often today's criminal makes peace with his conscience by saying: 'I steal,' he says, 'but I'm not going against the Church. I'm no enemy of Christ.' That's what today's criminal keeps telling himself, but once the Church takes the State's place, it'll be much harder for him to say, in defiance of the Church across the whole world, 'All men are mistaken, all are in error, all mankind is a false Church. I, a thief and a murderer, am the only true Christian Church.' That will be a hard thing to say to oneself; it takes a rare combination of unusual circumstances. Now look at it from the Church's own point of view on crime: isn't it bound to give up its present, almost pagan attitude—the mechanical amputation of its diseased member for the preservation of society, as it stands now—and instead fully and honestly take up the idea of the man's regeneration, his reform, his salvation?”

“What do you mean? I can't follow you again,” Miüsov broke in. “Some kind of dream again. Something shapeless, even incomprehensible. What is excommunication? What kind of exclusion is this? I suspect you're simply amusing yourself, Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, but you know, in reality it already is so,” the elder said suddenly, and everyone turned to him at once. “If it weren't for the Church of Christ, there'd be nothing to hold the criminal back from wrongdoing—no real punishment for it afterward, none, I mean, but the mechanical kind just mentioned, which in most cases only hardens the heart—and not the real punishment, the only effective one, the only one that deters and softens the heart, which lies in the recognition of sin by conscience.”
“How is that, if I may ask?” said Miüsov, with lively curiosity.

“Well,” the elder began, “all these sentences to exile at hard labor, and, in the old days, to flogging as well, reform no one, and, what's more, hardly deter a single criminal, and the number of crimes keeps rising rather than falling. You have to admit that. So the safety of society isn't actually being preserved, because although the offending member is mechanically cut off and sent far out of sight, another criminal always steps in to take his place at once—often two of them. If anything preserves society, even in our own time, and does regenerate and reform the criminal, it's only the law of Christ speaking in his conscience. Only by recognizing his own wrongdoing as a son of Christian society—that is, of the Church—does he recognize his sin against society—that is, against the Church. So it's only against the Church, and not against the State, that today's criminal can recognize he's sinned. If society, as a Church, had jurisdiction, it would know when to bring the excluded back and reunite them with itself. As things stand, the Church, having no real jurisdiction, but only the power of moral condemnation, withdraws of its own accord from actively punishing the criminal. It doesn't excommunicate him, but simply keeps up its motherly exhortation of him. What's more, the Church even tries to preserve full Christian communion with the criminal. It admits him to services, to the holy sacrament, gives him alms, treats him more like a captive than a convict. And what would become of the criminal, O Lord, if even Christian society—that is, the Church—rejected him the way civil law does, and cut him off too? What would become of him if the Church punished him with excommunication as the direct consequence of the secular sentence? There could be no more terrible despair, at least for a Russian criminal, since Russian criminals still have faith. Though who knows—perhaps then a fearful thing would happen, perhaps the despairing heart of the criminal would lose its faith, and then what would become of him? But the Church, like a tender, loving mother, holds back from active punishment herself, since the sinner has already been punished harshly enough by the civil law, and there must be at least someone left to pity him. Above all, the Church holds back because her judgment is the only one that contains the truth, and so it can't, in practice or in conscience, be joined to any other judgment, even as a temporary compromise. She can make no bargain about that. The foreign criminal, they say, rarely repents, because the very doctrines of our age confirm him in the belief that his crime isn't really a crime at all, but simply a reaction against an unjustly oppressive force. Society cuts him off entirely, through a force that mechanically triumphs over him and—so at least they say of themselves in Europe—carries out this exclusion along with hatred, forgetting him, and the deepest indifference to the ultimate fate of an erring brother. In this way, it all happens without any compassionate involvement from the Church, since in many cases there's no real church there at all—for though the clergy and the splendid church buildings remain, the churches themselves have long since striven to pass from Church into State and vanish into it completely. That, at least, seems to be how it is in Lutheran countries. As for Rome, it was proclaimed a State instead of a Church a thousand years ago. And so the criminal is no longer conscious of being a member of the Church, and sinks into despair. If he returns to society, it's often with such hatred that society itself instinctively casts him out again. You can judge for yourselves how that must end. In many respects it may seem the same here with us, but the difference is that, alongside the established courts, we also have the Church, which always keeps up its relationship with the criminal as a dear, still-precious son. And beyond that, there's still preserved, at least in thought, the judgment of the Church—no longer active in practice, but still alive as a dream for the future, and no doubt instinctively recognized by the criminal in his own soul. What was said here just now is true too—that if the Church's jurisdiction were actually introduced in full force, if the whole of society were changed into the Church, then not only would the Church's judgment have far more influence over the criminal's reform than it does now, but the crimes themselves might well be reduced almost beyond belief. And there's no doubt the Church would come to see the criminal, and the crime, of the future quite differently in many cases, and would succeed in restoring the excluded, restraining those planning evil, and regenerating the fallen. It's true,” Father Zossima said, with a smile, “that Christian society today isn't ready for this, and rests on only a handful of righteous men—but since they're never lacking, it will go on, unshaken, awaiting its complete transformation from a society still almost pagan in character into a single, universal, all-powerful Church. So be it, so be it! Even if it comes only at the end of the ages, for it is ordained to come to pass! And there's no need to fret over times and seasons, since the secret of the times and the seasons lies in the wisdom of God, in his foresight, in his love. And what looks, by human reckoning, still far off, may, by divine ordinance, already be close at hand, on the very eve of its coming. So be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy repeated, austere and reverent.
“Strange, extremely strange!” Miüsov said, not so much heatedly as with a kind of suppressed indignation.
“What strikes you as so strange?” Father Iosif asked cautiously.

“Why, it's beyond anything!” Miüsov suddenly burst out. “The State is eliminated, and the Church is raised up to take its place! It's not just Ultramontanism, it's arch-Ultramontanism! It's beyond even the dreams of Pope Gregory the Seventh!”

“You've got it completely backward,” Father Païssy said sternly. “Understand this: the Church is not to be transformed into the State. That's Rome's dream. That's the third temptation of the devil. It's the opposite—the State is to be transformed into the Church, is to rise and become a Church over the whole earth—which is the exact opposite of Ultramontanism and Rome, and of your interpretation, and is nothing less than the glorious destiny ordained for the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov fell into a pointed silence. His whole bearing conveyed an extraordinary sense of personal dignity. A superior, condescending smile played on his lips. Alyosha watched it all with his heart pounding. The whole conversation had stirred him deeply. He glanced over, in passing, at Rakitin, who stood motionless in his place by the door, watching and listening intently, though with lowered eyes. But the color in his cheeks told Alyosha that Rakitin was probably no less excited than he was, and Alyosha knew what was exciting him.

“Allow me to tell you a little anecdote, gentlemen,” Miüsov said, with a certain lofty air of importance. “A few years ago, not long after the December _coup d'état_, I happened to be calling in Paris on an extremely influential figure in the government, and I met a very interesting man at his house. This individual wasn't exactly a detective, but a sort of superintendent over an entire regiment of political detectives—a rather powerful post in its own way. Curiosity prompted me to seize the chance for a conversation with him. Since he hadn't come as a guest but as a subordinate official delivering a special report, and since he saw how his chief received me, he condescended to speak with a certain openness—within limits, of course. He was courteous rather than open, the way Frenchmen know how to be courteous, especially toward a foreigner. But I understood him thoroughly. The subject was the socialist revolutionaries, who were being hunted down at the time. I'll quote just one particularly striking remark this man dropped. 'We're not especially afraid,' he said, 'of all these socialists, anarchists, unbelievers, and revolutionaries; we keep an eye on them, we know all their movements. But there's a peculiar handful among them who believe in God, who are Christians, and yet are socialists too. Those are the ones we're most afraid of. They're dreadful people! A Christian socialist is far more to be feared than an atheist socialist.' Those words struck me at the time, and now, suddenly, they've come back to me here, gentlemen.”
“Are you applying them to us? Do you take us for socialists?” Father Païssy asked directly, without beating around the bush.

But before Pyotr Alexandrovitch could think what to answer, the door opened, and the long-awaited guest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, walked in. They'd more or less given up expecting him, and his sudden appearance caused a moment's surprise.

title: VI. Why Is Such A Man Alive?
paragraphs: Dmitri Fyodorovitch, a young man of twenty-eight, of medium height and pleasant appearance, looked older than his years. He was muscular, and showed clear signs of considerable physical strength. And yet there was something unhealthy about his face. It was rather thin, his cheeks hollow, with an unhealthy sallow tinge to them. His large, prominent, dark eyes had a look of firm resolve, and yet something vague in them too. Even when he was worked up, speaking irritably, his eyes somehow didn't follow his mood, but betrayed something else, sometimes quite out of keeping with what was happening at the moment. “It's hard to say what he's thinking,” people who spoke with him sometimes remarked. People who caught something brooding and sullen in his eyes would be startled by his sudden laugh, which spoke of cheerful, lighthearted thoughts at the very moment his eyes looked so gloomy. A certain strained look on his face was easy enough to explain at this particular moment. Everyone knew, or had heard, about the wildly restless, dissipated life he'd been leading lately, and about the violent rages that had flared up in his quarrels with his father. Several stories about it were making the rounds of town. It's true he was hot-tempered by nature, “of an unstable and unbalanced mind,” as our justice of the peace, Katchalnikov, had aptly put it.

He was dressed with style, impeccably, in a carefully buttoned frock coat. He wore black gloves and carried a top hat. Having only recently left the army, he still wore a mustache but no beard. His dark brown hair was cropped short and combed forward at the temples. He had the long, purposeful stride of a military man. He stood still for a moment on the threshold, glanced over the whole party, and went straight up to the elder, guessing correctly that he was their host. He gave him a low bow and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima rose from his chair and blessed him. Dmitri kissed his hand respectfully, with intense feeling—almost anger—and said:
“Be so kind as to forgive me for keeping you waiting so long, but Smerdyakov, the valet my father sent, told me twice, when I asked, that the appointment was for one o'clock. Now I suddenly learn—”
“Don't trouble yourself,” the elder interrupted. “It doesn't matter. You're a little late. It's of no consequence…”
“I'm extremely grateful to you, and expected nothing less from your kindness.”

Having said this, Dmitri bowed once more. Then, turning suddenly to his father, he gave him too a similarly low, respectful bow. He'd clearly planned this in advance, and made the bow in dead earnest, thinking it his duty to show his respect and good intentions.

Though Fyodor Pavlovitch had been caught off guard, he rose to the occasion. In answer to Dmitri's bow he leapt up from his chair and returned an equally low bow to his son. His face suddenly turned solemn and impressive, which gave him a downright malicious look. Dmitri bowed generally to everyone present, and without a word walked to the window with his long, determined stride, sat down in the one empty chair, beside Father Païssy, and, leaning forward, prepared to listen to the conversation he'd interrupted.
Dmitri's entrance had taken no more than two minutes, and the conversation resumed. But this time Miüsov decided it wasn't worth answering Father Païssy's persistent, almost irritable question.

“Allow me to bow out of this discussion,” he observed, with a certain well-bred nonchalance. “It's a delicate question too. Ivan Fyodorovitch is smiling at us over there. He must have something interesting to say about it as well. Ask him.”

“Nothing in particular, except one small remark,” Ivan answered at once. “European Liberals in general, and even our own liberal dilettantes, often mix up the ultimate results of socialism with those of Christianity. This bizarre notion is, of course, a characteristic feature of the type. But it's not only Liberals and dilettantes who confuse socialism with Christianity—in many cases, it seems, the police do too—the foreign police, that is. Your Paris anecdote is rather to the point, Pyotr Alexandrovitch.”

“I'll ask your permission to drop this subject entirely,” Miüsov repeated. “Instead I'll tell you, gentlemen, another interesting, rather characteristic anecdote about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he solemnly declared, in the course of an argument, that there was nothing whatever in the whole world to make men love their neighbors. That there's no law of nature requiring man to love mankind, and that if there has ever been any love on earth, it hasn't been owing to any natural law, but simply because men believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added, in passing, that the whole of natural law lies in that belief, and that if you destroyed the belief in immortality in mankind, not only love but every living force sustaining the life of the world would instantly dry up. What's more, nothing would then be immoral—everything would be permitted, even cannibalism. And that's not all. He ended by asserting that for every individual, like ourselves, who doesn't believe in God or in immortality, the moral law of nature must immediately flip into the exact opposite of the old religious law, and that self-interest, even carried to crime, must become not merely permissible, but recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable, outcome of his situation. From this paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of our eccentric, paradox-loving friend Ivan Fyodorovitch's theories.”
“Excuse me,” Dmitri suddenly cried, “if I've heard right, crime must not only be permitted but even recognized as the inevitable, most rational outcome for every unbeliever! Is that it, or not?”
“Quite so,” said Father Païssy.
“I'll remember that.”
Having said these words, Dmitri fell silent as abruptly as he'd spoken. Everyone looked at him with curiosity.
“Is that really your conviction about what follows from the disappearance of faith in immortality?” the elder suddenly asked Ivan.
“Yes. That was my argument. There's no virtue at all, if there's no immortality.”
“You're blessed to believe that—or else deeply unhappy.”
“Why unhappy?” Ivan asked, smiling.
“Because, in all likelihood, you don't believe it yourself—not in the immortality of your own soul, and not in what you wrote in your article on Church jurisdiction, either.”
“Perhaps you're right!… But I wasn't entirely joking,” Ivan confessed suddenly, strangely, flushing quickly.

“You weren't entirely joking. That's true. The question is still gnawing at your heart, unanswered. But the martyr sometimes likes to amuse himself with his own despair—as if driven to it by the despair itself. In the meantime, in your despair, you amuse yourself too, with magazine articles and drawing-room debates, though you don't believe your own arguments, and mock them inwardly with an aching heart… That question hasn't been answered, and it's your great sorrow, because it's crying out for an answer.”
“But can it be answered—by me? Answered in the affirmative?” Ivan went on asking, oddly, still looking at the elder with that same inexplicable smile.

“If it can't be settled in the affirmative, it will never be settled in the negative either. You know that's the peculiar nature of your heart, and all its suffering comes from that.
