But thank the Creator who gave you a lofty heart, capable of such suffering—of thinking, of seeking higher things—for our dwelling place is in the heavens. God grant that your heart find its answer while still on earth, and may God bless your path.”

The elder raised his hand and would have made the sign of the cross over Ivan from where he stood. But Ivan rose from his seat, went up to him, received his blessing, and, kissing his hand, went back to his place in silence. His face looked firm and serious. This gesture, and the whole preceding conversation—so surprising, coming from Ivan—struck everyone with its strangeness, its air of solemnity, so that they all fell silent for a moment, and something like apprehension showed on Alyosha's face. But Miüsov suddenly shrugged his shoulders. And at that same instant Fyodor Pavlovitch jumped up from his seat.

“Most pious, most holy elder,” he cried, pointing to Ivan, “that is my son, flesh of my flesh, the dearest of my flesh! He's my most dutiful Karl Moor, so to speak, while this other son, who's just come in, Dmitri, against whom I'm seeking justice from you, is the undutiful Franz Moor—they're both straight out of Schiller's _Robbers_, and so I'm the reigning Count von Moor! Judge us and save us! We need not only your prayers, but your prophecies!”

“Speak without clowning around, and don't start by insulting the members of your own family,” the elder answered, in a faint, exhausted voice. He was plainly growing more and more tired, his strength failing him.

“An unseemly farce, exactly what I expected when I came here!” Dmitri cried, indignant. He too leapt to his feet. “Forgive it, reverend Father,” he added, turning to the elder. “I'm not an educated man, I don't even know the proper way to address you, but you've been deceived, and you were too kind, letting us meet here at all. All my father wants is a scandal. Only he could tell you why. He always has some motive. But I think I know why—”

“They all blame me, every one of them!” Fyodor Pavlovitch broke in. “Pyotr Alexandrovitch here blames me too. You've been blaming me, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you have!” he suddenly turned on Miüsov, though Miüsov hadn't dreamed of interrupting him. “They all accuse me of hiding the children's money in my boots, of cheating them—but isn't there a court of law? There they'll work it all out for you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, from your own notes, your letters, your agreements, exactly how much money you had, how much you've spent, and how much is left. Why does Pyotr Alexandrovitch refuse to sit in judgment? Dmitri's no stranger to him. Because they're all against me, while Dmitri Fyodorovitch is in debt to me—and not a little, but several thousand, which I have documentary proof of. The whole town is buzzing with his debaucheries. And back where he was stationed before, he spent a thousand or two several times over on the seduction of some respectable girl or other—we know all about that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, down to the most private details. I'll prove it… Would you believe it, holy Father, he won the heart of one of the most honorable young ladies of good family and fortune, the daughter of a gallant colonel, formerly his commanding officer, a man decorated with the Order of St. Anna. He compromised the girl with a promise of marriage, and now she's an orphan, here in town, betrothed to him—and right in front of her he's dancing attendance on a certain enchantress. And although this enchantress has been living in what you might call a civil marriage with a respectable man, she has an independent streak, an unapproachable fortress to everyone else—just like a lawful wife—because she's virtuous, yes, holy Fathers, virtuous. Dmitri Fyodorovitch wants to unlock this fortress with a golden key, and that's why he's being insolent to me now, trying to squeeze money out of me, even though he's already thrown away thousands on this enchantress. He's constantly borrowing money for the purpose. From whom, do you suppose? Shall I say, Mitya?”
“Be quiet!” cried Dmitri. “Wait till I'm gone. Don't you dare, in my presence, slander the good name of an honorable girl! That you'd even say a word about her is an outrage, and I won't allow it!”
He was out of breath.
“Mitya! Mitya!” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried hysterically, squeezing out a tear. “And your father's blessing means nothing to you? What if I curse you—what then?”
“Shameless hypocrite!” Dmitri exclaimed furiously.

“He says that to his own father! his father! What would he be like with others? Gentlemen, just imagine—there's a poor but honorable man living here, weighed down by a large family, a captain who got into trouble and was discharged from the army—not publicly, not by court-martial, no stain on his honor. And three weeks ago Dmitri grabbed him by the beard in a tavern, dragged him out into the street, and beat him publicly, all because the man does a bit of business on my behalf.”

“It's all a lie! Outwardly the truth, maybe, but a lie underneath!” Dmitri was shaking with rage. “Father, I'm not defending what I did. Yes, I admit it publicly—I behaved like a brute to that captain, and I regret it now, I'm disgusted with myself for my brutal rage. But this captain, this agent of yours, went to that lady you call an enchantress, and suggested to her, on your behalf, that she take my I.O.U.'s—which you had in your possession—and sue me over them, to have me thrown in prison, in case I kept demanding an accounting of my property from you. Now you accuse me of a weakness for that lady, when it was you who put her up to captivating me! She told me so herself, to my face… She told me the whole story and laughed at you for it… You wanted to put me in prison because you're jealous of me over her, because you'd started forcing your attentions on her too—I know all about that as well; she laughed at you for that too, you hear—she laughed at you telling me about it. So here you have him, this man, this father reproaching his profligate son! Gentlemen, forgive my anger, but I saw it coming—that this crafty old man would only bring us together here to make a scene. I came ready to forgive him, if he offered his hand—to forgive him, and to ask his forgiveness! But since he's just this minute insulted not only me but an honorable young lady, whom I hold in such reverence I don't dare take her name in vain, I've decided to expose his game, whatever he is to me—”

He couldn't go on. His eyes were blazing and he was struggling to breathe. But everyone in the cell was shaken. Everyone except Father Zossima rose uneasily from their seats. The monks looked stern, but waited for guidance from the elder. He sat perfectly still, pale, not from excitement but from the weakness of illness. A pleading smile lit up his face; every so often he raised his hand, as if to check the storm, and, of course, a single gesture from him would have been enough to end the scene; but he seemed to be waiting for something, watching them all intently, as if trying to make out something not entirely clear to him. At last Miüsov felt utterly humiliated and disgraced.

“We're all to blame for this scandalous scene,” he said hotly. “But I didn't foresee it when I came here, even though I knew who I was dealing with. This has to be stopped, right now! Believe me, your reverence, I had no precise knowledge of the details that have just come out—I was unwilling to believe them, and I'm learning of them for the first time… A father jealous of his own son's relations with a woman of loose conduct, scheming with the creature to get his son thrown in prison! And this is the company I've been forced to be seen in! I've been deceived. I declare to you all that I've been deceived as much as anyone.”

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly howled, in an unnatural voice, “if you weren't my son, I'd challenge you to a duel this instant—with pistols, at three paces—across a handkerchief,” he finished, stamping both feet.

With old liars who've spent their whole lives acting, there are moments when they slip so completely into the part that they actually tremble, or shed real tears of emotion, even while, at that very moment, or a second later, they're able to whisper to themselves: “You know you're lying, you shameless old sinner! You're performing right now, in spite of your 'holy' rage.”
Dmitri frowned painfully, and looked at his father with unutterable contempt.

“I thought… I thought,” he said, in a soft, oddly controlled voice, “that I was coming back to my birthplace with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to look after him in his old age, and instead I find nothing but a depraved libertine, a despicable clown!”

“A duel!” the old wretch howled again, breathless, spitting out each syllable. “And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, let me tell you—there's never been a nobler, more honest woman in your whole family—you hear me—more honest than this 'creature,' as you've dared to call her! And you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you abandoned your betrothed for that 'creature,' so you must have already decided your betrothed couldn't hold a candle to her yourself. That's the kind of woman being called a 'creature'!”
“Shameful!” burst from Father Iosif.
“Shameful and disgraceful!” Kalganov cried in a boyish voice, flushing crimson, trembling with emotion. He'd been silent until that moment.

“Why is such a man even alive?” Dmitri growled in a hollow voice, beside himself with rage, hunching his shoulders until he looked almost deformed. “Tell me, can he really be allowed to go on defiling the earth?” He looked around at everyone, pointing at the old man. He spoke evenly, deliberately.

“Listen to him, monks, listen to the parricide!” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, rushing at Father Iosif. “That's your answer to your 'shameful!' What's shameful? That 'creature,' that 'woman of loose conduct,' is perhaps holier than you are yourselves—you monks, seeking your salvation! She may have fallen in her youth, ruined by her circumstances. But she loved much, and Christ himself forgave the woman 'who loved much.'”
“It wasn't for love of that kind that Christ forgave her,” Father Iosif broke in, gentle but impatient.
“Yes, it was, monks, it was for that very kind! You save your souls here, eating cabbage, and think you're the righteous. You eat a minnow a day and think you can bribe God with a minnow.”
“This is unbearable!” came from all sides in the cell.

But this unseemly scene was cut short in the most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Nearly frantic with worry for the elder and for everyone else, Alyosha still managed to catch him by the arm and support him. Father Zossima moved toward Dmitri, and, reaching him, sank to his knees before him. Alyosha thought he'd simply collapsed from weakness, but that wasn't it. The elder deliberately, distinctly bowed down at Dmitri's feet, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so stunned he failed even to help him back up. There was a faint smile on the elder's lips.
“Good-bye! Forgive me, all of you!” he said, bowing to his guests on every side.

Dmitri stood frozen for a few moments in astonishment. Bowing down to him like that—what could it mean? Suddenly he cried out, “Oh, God!”, buried his face in his hands, and rushed from the room. All the guests streamed out after him, in the confusion forgetting to say good-bye or bow to their host. Only the monks went up to him again for a blessing.

“What did that mean, falling at his feet like that? Was it symbolic, or what?” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, suddenly subdued, trying to strike up conversation again without quite daring to address anyone in particular. They were all just then passing out of the hermitage grounds.
“I can't speak for madhouses and madmen,” Miüsov answered at once, ill-humored, “but I'll spare myself your company, Fyodor Pavlovitch—for good, trust me. Where's that monk?”

“That monk”—the one who'd invited them to dine with the Superior—hadn't kept them waiting. He met them the moment they came down the steps from the elder's cell, as though he'd been waiting there the whole time.

“Reverend Father, kindly do me a favor. Convey my deepest respects to the Father Superior, and apologize for me, personally, Miüsov, to his reverence, and tell him that, owing to unforeseen circumstances, I deeply regret being unable to have the honor of joining his table, much as I would like to,” Miüsov said irritably to the monk.

“And that unforeseen circumstance, of course, is me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in at once. “Do you hear, Father? This gentleman doesn't want to stay in my company, or he'd come at once. And off you go, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, do go to the Father Superior, and good appetite to you. I'll decline, not you. Home, home, I'll eat at home, I don't feel up to it here, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, my amiable relative.”
“I'm not your relative, and never have been, you contemptible man!”

“I said it on purpose to rile you, because you always deny the relationship, though you really are one, whatever your dodging. I'll prove it from the church calendar. As for you, Ivan, stay if you like. I'll send the horses for you later. Propriety requires you to go to the Father Superior, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to apologize for the disturbance we've caused…”
“Is it true you're going home? Aren't you lying?”

“Pyotr Alexandrovitch! How could I dare, after what's just happened! Forgive me, gentlemen, I got carried away! And I'm upset besides! And, truly, I'm ashamed. Gentlemen, one man has the heart of Alexander of Macedon, and another the heart of the little dog Fido. Mine is the heart of the little dog Fido. I'm ashamed! After a scene like that, how could I go to dinner and gobble up the monastery's sauces? I'm ashamed, I can't do it. You must excuse me!”

“The devil only knows—what if he's tricking us?” Miüsov thought, still hesitating, watching the retreating buffoon with distrustful eyes. Fyodor Pavlovitch turned around, and, noticing Miüsov watching him, blew him a kiss.
“Well, are you coming to the Superior's?” Miüsov asked Ivan abruptly.
“Why not? I was specially invited yesterday.”

“Unfortunately I feel obliged to go to this wretched dinner,” Miüsov said, still irritated, not caring that the monk was listening. “We ought, at least, to apologize for the disturbance, and explain that none of it was our doing. What do you think?”
“Yes, we should explain it wasn't our doing. Besides, father won't be there,” Ivan observed.
“Well, I should hope not! Confound this dinner!”

They all walked on, all the same. The monk listened in silence. On the way through the copse he made one remark, that the Father Superior had been waiting a long time, and they were already more than half an hour late. He got no answer. Miüsov looked at Ivan with something like hatred.
“There he goes, off to dinner as though nothing had happened,” he thought. “A brazen face, and the conscience of a Karamazov!”

title: VII. A Young Man Bent On A Career
paragraphs: Alyosha helped Father Zossima to his bedroom and sat him down on the bed. It was a small room, furnished with the barest necessities. There was a narrow iron bedstead with a strip of felt for a mattress. In the corner, under the icons, stood a reading desk with a cross and the Gospel lying on it. The elder sank onto the bed, exhausted. His eyes glittered and he breathed hard. He looked intently at Alyosha, as if weighing something.
“Go, my dear boy, go. Porfiry is enough for me. Hurry, you're needed there—go and wait on the Father Superior's table.”
“Let me stay here,” Alyosha pleaded.

“You're more needed there. There's no peace there. You'll wait on them, and be of use. If evil spirits rise up, say a prayer. And remember, my son”—the elder liked to call him that—“this isn't the place for you, going forward. When it's God's will to call me, leave the monastery. Go away for good.”
Alyosha flinched.

“What is it? This isn't your place, not for now. I bless you for great service out in the world. Yours will be a long pilgrimage. And you'll have to take a wife, too. You'll have to bear _everything_ before you come back. There'll be much to do. But I have no doubts about you, and that's why I'm sending you out. Christ is with you. Don't abandon him, and he won't abandon you. You'll see great sorrow, and in that sorrow you'll be happy. This is my last message to you: seek happiness in sorrow. Work, work without ceasing. Remember my words, because though I'll speak with you again, my hours, not just my days, are numbered now.”
Alyosha's face again betrayed a strong emotion. The corners of his mouth trembled.

“What is it now?” Father Zossima asked, smiling gently. “The worldly follow their dead with tears, but here we rejoice over the father who's departing. We rejoice, and we pray for him. Leave me now, I must pray. Go, and hurry. Stay close to your brothers. Not just one of them—both.”

Father Zossima raised his hand to bless him. Alyosha couldn't argue, though he longed with all his heart to stay. He longed, too, to ask what it meant, that bow to Dmitri—the question was right on the tip of his tongue—but he didn't dare ask it. He knew the elder would have explained it unasked, if he'd thought it right. But clearly it wasn't his will to do so. That action had left a terrible impression on Alyosha; he believed, without question, in its mysterious meaning. Mysterious, and perhaps dreadful.

Hurrying out of the hermitage grounds to reach the monastery in time to serve at the Father Superior's dinner, he suddenly felt a stab at his heart, and stopped short. He seemed to hear again Father Zossima's words, foretelling his own approaching end. Whatever he'd foretold so exactly was bound to come true. Alyosha believed that without question. But how could he be left without him? How could he go on living without seeing him, without hearing him? Where would he go? The elder had told him not to weep, and to leave the monastery. Good God! It had been a long time since Alyosha had felt such anguish. He hurried through the copse that separated the monastery from the hermitage, and, unable to bear the weight of his own thoughts, gazed at the ancient pines lining the path. He hadn't far to go—about five hundred paces. He didn't expect to meet anyone at that hour, but at the first bend in the path he noticed Rakitin. He was waiting for someone.
“Waiting for me?” Alyosha asked, catching up with him.

“That's right,” grinned Rakitin. “You're hurrying off to the Father Superior, I know—he's got a banquet on. There hasn't been a banquet like it since the Superior entertained the Bishop and General Pahatov—remember that one? I won't be there, but you go on and pass the sauces. Tell me one thing, Alexey—what does that vision mean? That's what I want to ask you.”
“What vision?”
“That bowing to your brother, Dmitri. And didn't he knock his forehead on the ground while he was at it!”
“You mean Father Zossima?”
“Yes, Father Zossima.”
“Knocked his forehead on the ground?”
“Ah, an irreverent way to put it! Well, never mind that—what does the vision mean, anyway?”
“I don't know what it means, Misha.”

“I knew he wouldn't explain it to you! There's nothing remarkable about it, of course—just the usual holy mummery. But there was a purpose behind the performance. All the pious folk in town will talk about it, spread the story through the whole province, wondering what it meant. To my mind, the old man really does have a sharp nose—he's sniffed out a crime. Your household reeks of it.”
“What crime?”
Rakitin clearly had something he was itching to say.

“It'll be in your family, this crime. Between your brothers and your rich old father. So Father Zossima flopped down, ready for whatever comes. If something happens later on, it'll be, 'Ah, the holy man foresaw it, prophesied it!'—though it's a pretty poor sort of prophecy, flopping down like that. 'Ah, but it was symbolic,' they'll say, 'an allegory,' and the devil knows what else! It'll be remembered to his glory: 'He predicted the crime and marked out the criminal!' That's always the way with these crazy fanatics—they cross themselves in the tavern and throw stones at the temple. Just like your elder—takes a stick to an honest man and falls at the feet of a murderer.”
“What crime? What murderer? What are you talking about?”
Alyosha stopped dead. Rakitin stopped too.

“What murderer? As if you didn't know! I'd bet you've thought about it before. That's interesting too, by the way. Listen, Alyosha—you always tell the truth, even if you're always sitting on the fence. Have you thought of it or not? Answer me.”
“I have,” Alyosha answered quietly. Even Rakitin was taken aback.
“What? You really have?” he cried.
“I—I haven't exactly thought it through,” Alyosha muttered, “but the moment you started talking so strangely, I felt as though I'd thought of it myself.”
“You see? (And how well you put it, too!) Looking at your father and your brother Mitya today, you thought of a crime. So I'm not mistaken, then?”
“But wait, wait a moment,” Alyosha broke in uneasily. “What's led you to see all this? Why does it interest you? That's the first question.”

“Two separate questions, but both natural. I'll take them one at a time. What led me to see it? I wouldn't have seen it at all if I hadn't suddenly understood your brother Dmitri—seen right into the heart of him, all at once. I caught the whole man from a single trait. Honest but passionate men like him have a line that mustn't be crossed. Cross it, and he'd run at your father with a knife. But your father's a drunken, degenerate old sinner who's never been able to find that line—if the two of them let themselves go, they'll both come to grief.”
“No, Misha, no. If that's all, you've set my mind at rest. It won't come to that.”

“Then why are you trembling? Let me tell you—he may be honest, our Mitya (stupid, but honest), but he's a sensualist. That's the very definition of him, the core of his nature. It's your father who's passed his low sensuality down to him. Do you know, I genuinely wonder at you, Alyosha, how you've managed to stay so pure. You're a Karamazov too, you know! In your family sensuality runs like a disease. Now these three sensualists are watching each other, knives tucked in their belts. The three of them, butting heads together, and you might make a fourth.”
“You're wrong about that woman. Dmitri—he despises her,” said Alyosha, with something like a shudder.

“Grushenka? No, brother, he doesn't despise her. Since he's openly thrown over his betrothed for her, he can't despise her. There's something here, my dear boy, that you don't understand yet. A man falls in love with some beauty—with a woman's body, or even just a part of a woman's body (a sensualist would understand that)—and he'll abandon his own children for her, sell his father and mother, sell his own country, Russia, to boot. If he's honest, he'll steal; if he's kind, he'll murder; if he's faithful, he'll betray. Pushkin, the poet of women's feet, sang their praises in verse. Others don't write poems about them, but they can't look at a woman's feet without a thrill—and it's not only the feet. Contempt's no defense here, brother, even if he really did despise Grushenka. He does—but he can't tear himself away from her.”
“I understand that,” Alyosha said suddenly, the words slipping out.

“Really? Well, I daresay you do understand, since it slipped out of you so easily,” said Rakitin, with a touch of malice. “That came out without your meaning it to, and the confession's all the more precious for that. So it's a familiar subject—you've thought about it before, then, about sensuality, I mean! Oh, you innocent soul! You're a quiet one, Alyosha, a saint, I know that, but the devil only knows what you've thought about, what you already know! You're pure, but you've been down into the depths… I've been watching you a long time. You're a Karamazov yourself, through and through—no doubt breeding and blood have something to answer for. A sensualist from your father, a crazy saint from your mother. Why are you trembling? So it's true, then? You know, Grushenka's been begging me to bring you along. 'I'll pull off his cassock,' she says. You can't imagine how she keeps after me to bring you. I wondered why she took such an interest in you. Do you know, she's an extraordinary woman too!”
“Thank her, and tell her I'm not coming,” Alyosha said, with a strained smile. “Finish what you were saying, Misha. I'll tell you my thoughts after.”

“There's nothing left to finish. It's all perfectly clear. Same old tune, brother. If even you're a sensualist at heart, what about your brother Ivan? He's a Karamazov too. What's at the root of all you Karamazovs is that you're all sensual, grasping, and crazy! Your brother Ivan writes theological articles as a joke, for some idiotic, unknown reason of his own, even though he's an atheist and admits himself it's a fraud—that's your brother Ivan for you. He's trying to steal Mitya's betrothed for himself, and I suspect he'll manage it, too. And what's more, it's with Mitya's own consent. Because Mitya will hand his betrothed over to him just to be rid of her, and escape to Grushenka. And he's ready to do exactly that, for all his fine talk of nobility and disinterest. Mark that. Those are the most dangerous people of all! Who the devil can make sense of him? He knows he's vile, and goes right on being vile! And let me tell you something else—the old man, your father, is standing in Mitya's way right now too. He's suddenly gone mad over Grushenka. His mouth waters at the sight of her. It's entirely on her account that he made that scene in the cell just now, simply because Miüsov called her an 'abandoned creature.' He's worse than a tomcat in heat. At first he only used her in connection with his taverns and some other shady business of his, but now he's suddenly woken up to what she really is, and he's gone wild over her. He keeps pestering her with offers—not honorable ones, of course. And the two of them, father and son, are going to collide on that path, the precious pair! But Grushenka favors neither of them—she's still playing with them both, teasing them, weighing which one she can get more out of. Because even though she could squeeze a lot of money out of the old man, he wouldn't marry her, and he might turn stingy in the end and shut his purse. That's where Mitya's value comes in—he's got no money, but he's ready to marry her. Yes, ready to marry her! To throw over his betrothed, a rare beauty, Katerina Ivanovna—rich, a colonel's daughter—and marry Grushenka instead, who's been the mistress of a dissolute old merchant, Samsonov, a coarse, uneducated small-town power broker. Some murderous collision might well come out of all this, and that's exactly what your brother Ivan is waiting for. It would suit him down to the ground. He'll carry off Katerina Ivanovna, whom he's pining for, and pocket her dowry of sixty thousand. That's a nice start for a man of no consequence and no money. And take note—he won't be wronging Mitya at all, he'll be doing him the greatest service. Because I know for a fact that just last week Mitya, drunk in a tavern with some gypsy girls, cried out loud that he wasn't worthy of his betrothed, Katya, but that his brother Ivan—now he was the one who deserved her. And Katerina Ivanovna won't, in the end, turn down such a fascinating man as Ivan. She's already torn between the two of them. And how has this Ivan won all of you over, so that you all worship him? He's laughing at you, that's what, and enjoying himself at your expense.”
“How do you know? How can you speak so confidently?” Alyosha asked sharply, frowning.
“Why do you ask, if my answer scares you? It shows you know I'm telling the truth.”
“You don't like Ivan. Ivan wouldn't be tempted by money.”
“Really? And by Katerina Ivanovna's beauty? It's not just the money, though sixty thousand is quite an attraction on its own.”
“Ivan is above all that. He wouldn't curry favor with anyone for thousands. It's not money Ivan's after, not comfort. Maybe it's suffering he's after.”
“What wild dream is this now? Oh, you—aristocrats!”
“Ah, Misha, he has a stormy spirit. His mind is in chains. He's haunted by some great, unresolved doubt. He's one of those people who don't want millions—they want an answer to their questions.”

“That's plagiarism, Alyosha. You're quoting your elder's own phrases. Ah, Ivan's set you a nice little riddle, hasn't he!” Rakitin cried, with unconcealed spite. His face changed, his lips twitched. “And it's a stupid riddle, too. No point guessing it. Rack your brains all you like—you'll see. His article's absurd, ridiculous. And did you hear that idiotic theory of his just now—if there's no immortality of the soul, then there's no virtue, and everything's permitted. (And by the way, do you remember how your brother Mitya cried out, 'I'll remember!') A fine theory for scoundrels!—(I'm being abusive, that's stupid of me.) Not for scoundrels, but for pedantic _poseurs_, 'haunted by profound, unsolved doubts.' He's showing off, that's all—and what it all boils down to is 'on the one hand we cannot but admit' and 'on the other it must be confessed!' His whole theory's a fraud! Humanity will find within itself the strength to live for virtue even without believing in immortality. It'll find it in the love of freedom, of equality, of brotherhood.”
Rakitin could hardly contain himself, worked up as he was, but suddenly, as if remembering something, he stopped short.
“Well, that's enough of that,” he said, with an even more crooked smile. “Why are you laughing? Do you think I'm just a vulgar fool?”

“No, I never once thought you a vulgar fool. You're clever, but—never mind, I was silly to smile. I understand why you're getting hot about it, Misha. I gather from all this heat that you're not exactly indifferent to Katerina Ivanovna yourself—I've suspected that for a while now, brother, that's why you don't like my brother Ivan. Are you jealous of him?”
“And jealous of her money too, why not add that?”
“I won't say anything about the money. I'm not trying to insult you.”

“I'll take your word for it, but the devil take you, and your brother Ivan along with you. Don't you understand that a man might dislike him quite apart from Katerina Ivanovna? And why the devil should I like him, anyway? He condescends to insult me, you know. Why shouldn't I have the right to insult him back?”
“I've never heard him say anything about you, good or bad. He doesn't mention you at all.”

“But I heard that the day before yesterday, at Katerina Ivanovna's, he was tearing me apart for all he was worth—so you see how much interest he takes in your humble servant. And after that, I couldn't say which of us is really the jealous one, brother. He was so good as to give the opinion that, if I don't go in for an archimandrite's career sometime soon and become a monk, I'm sure to go off to Petersburg and land a spot on some respectable magazine as a reviewer, that I'll write for the next ten years, and eventually end up owning the magazine myself, and bring it out on the liberal, atheistic side, with a socialist tinge—a faint gloss of socialism, mind you, while keeping a sharp eye on both sides the whole time, playing both ends against the middle and fooling the fools. According to your brother's account, that little tinge of socialism won't stop me from putting the profits away and investing them, under the guidance of some Jewish financier, until by the end of my career I build a great house in Petersburg and move my publishing offices into it, letting out the upper floors to lodgers. He's even picked the spot for it—near the new stone bridge across the Neva, the one they say is going to be built in Petersburg.”
“Ah, Misha, that's exactly what will actually happen, every word of it,” Alyosha cried, unable to hold back a good-humored smile.
“You're pleased to be sarcastic too, are you, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

“No, no, I'm joking, forgive me. I've got something else entirely on my mind. But excuse me—who could have told you all this? You can't have been at Katerina Ivanovna's yourself while he was talking about you?”

“I wasn't there, but Dmitri Fyodorovitch was, and I heard him tell it with my own ears—if you want to know, he didn't tell me directly, I overheard him, quite by accident, of course, since I was sitting in Grushenka's bedroom and couldn't leave because Dmitri Fyodorovitch was in the next room.”
“Oh, right, I'd forgotten she was a relation of yours.”
“A relation! That Grushenka, a relation of mine!” Rakitin cried, turning crimson. “Are you out of your mind? Have you lost your senses?”
“Why, isn't she a relation of yours? I heard she was.”

“Where on earth could you have heard that? You Karamazovs go around bragging about being an ancient noble family, when your own father used to run around playing the buffoon at other men's tables, barely let into the kitchen as a favor. I may only be a priest's son, dirt in the eyes of noblemen like you, but don't insult me so lightly, so carelessly. I have a sense of honor too, Alexey Fyodorovitch—I couldn't possibly be related to Grushenka, a common harlot. I'd like you to understand that!”
Rakitin was thoroughly worked up.

“Forgive me, for goodness' sake, I had no idea… besides… how can you call her a harlot? Is she… that sort of woman?” Alyosha suddenly flushed. “I tell you again, I heard she was a relation of yours. You go to see her often, and you told me yourself you're not her lover. I never dreamed you, of all people, had such contempt for her! Does she really deserve it?”

“I may have my own reasons for visiting her. That's none of your business. But as for being related to her, your brother—or even your father, for that matter—is far more likely to make her family than I am. Well, here we are. You'd better go on to the kitchen. Hullo! What's wrong, what's happening? Are we late? They can't have finished dinner already! Have the Karamazovs been making trouble again? No doubt they have. There's your father, and your brother Ivan right behind him. They've broken away from the Father Superior's. And look, there's Father Isidor shouting something after them from the steps. And your father's shouting too, waving his arms around. I'd guess he's cursing. Bah, and there's Miüsov driving off in his carriage. You see, he's leaving. And there's old Maximov running!—there must have been a row. There can't have been any dinner at all. Surely they haven't been beating up the Father Superior! Or have they been the ones beaten? It'd serve them right, either way!”
